**A note on the premise:** The delegation states that Massachusetts required no vital registration until 1841 and that "nothing civil exists" for 1820–1850. It states town- and city-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was ordered as early as **1639** and continued at the **town** level throughout the colonial and early national period; 1841 marks only the start of a **centralized statewide** recording system layered on top of the pre-existing town series. In other words, town clerks in Berkshire County towns were keeping — or were supposed to be keeping — vital entries well before 1841, and these town registers (many compiled and published as "Vital Records of [Town] to 1850") are themselves a civil record set. This guide therefore treats town vital records, alongside church registers and cemetery inscriptions, as a primary source for 1820–1850. That said, church registers and cemetery inscriptions remain central, since pre-1841 town compliance was uneven and church/burial entries often fill the gaps town clerks left.

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
County Cork is within the province of Munster. No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in the 1830s–1840s — this is a critical planning point.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary substitute for vital records)*
- **Roman Catholic parish registers** (baptisms and marriages; burials rarely kept) are the core source. Many Cork parishes begin in the 1810s–1830s. The **National Library of Ireland** holds free online images of Catholic registers up to 1880.
- **Church of Ireland (Anglican) registers** are held by the Representative Church Body Library and in local custody.

> ⚠️ Civil registration of births and deaths did not begin until **1 January 1864**; non-Catholic marriages only from **1845**. There are no birth or death certificates to find for the 1830s–1840s — go straight to church registers.

---

### Census Substitutes
No national census survives for the 1830s–1840s — most pre-1901 returns were destroyed in the **1922 Four Courts fire**. The standard substitutes are:

| Record | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Tithe Applotment Books** | 1823–1837 | Lists occupiers of tithe-liable land — the core census substitute for your exact decade |
| **Griffith's Valuation** | Early 1850s | Lists every householder; nearest full-population snapshot after your period |

---

### Land Records
- Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) cover land occupancy for this period.

### Immigration / Emigration Records
- Passenger manifests from Cork's ports (**Cobh/Queenstown**) during the Famine period list complete family groups including infants — always check the full manifest, not just the head of household.

### Other Record Types
- Cemetery records, newspaper archives, probate records, and military records were not confirmed with Cork-specific coverage by this survey. The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed many wills and government records generally.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland | Catholic parish register images to 1880 | Free online |
| Representative Church Body Library | Church of Ireland parish registers | In-person / named by wiki |
| Find A Grave | General cemetery index | Free |
| Newspapers.com | General newspaper archive | Subscription |

---

## Known Record Losses
The **1922 Four Courts fire** destroyed most pre-1901 Irish census returns and many wills and government records. The Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation are the standard substitutes named in the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)).

---

## Recommended Next Steps
1. **Identify the specific parish or townland** your ancestor came from — use the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) or Griffith's Valuation to pin this down.
2. **Search that parish's Catholic church register** via the National Library of Ireland's free image service.
3. **Check Cork emigration manifests** from Cobh/Queenstown — scan the whole manifest for the entire family group.
4. Once you have a parish name, a follow-up catalog search specifically by parish is likely to surface more resources.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Kolonica, Slovakia (1700s-1890s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Modern municipality:** Kolonica, Snina District, Slovakia.
- **Historical jurisdiction, target period:** The village's own FamilySearch Catalog entry (koha:727653) identifies it as 'formerly Kolonica, Zemplén, Hungary' — so for 1700s-1890s research the relevant civil/ecclesiastical jurisdiction is Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary, not modern Slovakia.
- **Boundary history:** place_search returns four successive standard jurisdictions for this single village — Kolonica, Snina, Czechoslovakia (1922-1960); Kolonica, Humenné, Czechoslovakia (1960-1993); Kolonica, Humenné, Slovakia (1993-1996); Kolonica, Snina, Slovakia (1993-present) — none reaching back into the 1700s-1890s target period, confirming the Hungarian-era administration applied then.
- This survey's place-level tools (place_population, wiki_place_page x4, collections_search, volume_search) returned no usable data for this specific village; see Quirks.

## Boundary changes
- Kolonica moved between Snina and Humenné districts/jurisdiction names across the 20th century (see dates above) but these changes post-date the 1700s-1890s research window.
- Before 1918 (and so throughout the target period) the village was administered as part of Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary, per the catalog's own description of the parish's former affiliation.

## Available record types

### Church records
- **Denomination present:** Greek Catholic (Gréckokatolícka cirkev), per the FamilySearch Catalog entry's creator field, 'Grécko-katolícka cirkev. Farský úrad Kolonica (Snina)'.
- **Record types and coverage:** A single catalog entry (koha:727653), 'Cirkevná matrika, 1824-1924', covers baptisms, marriages and deaths. Film 1792766 (image group 4406755) holds: baptisms 1824-1833, marriages 1825-1833, deaths 1824-1833, and baptisms 1890-1922 (inventory nos. 460-461). Film 1792767 (image group 4405907) continues: baptisms 1922-1924, marriages 1890-1924, deaths 1890-1924.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library and Granite Mountain Record Vault hold the microfilm copies; the catalog marks the collection 'availableOnline: true' with a pointer to familysearch.org/search/collection/1554443 (noting images for film 1793684 specifically are NOT available).
- **Gap:** The catalog's own register run shows baptisms for 1824-1833 and then 1890-1922, with no indication in the returned record of a continuously covered run in between (e.g., 1834-1889) — this survey could not confirm whether that intervening span survives; check the full film/collection directly rather than assuming a gap or assuming continuity.
- **Earliest point reached:** 1824. No tool result in this survey found an earlier Kolonica register reaching back into the 1700s; the catalog's title itself begins '1824-1924', so earlier 18th-century church records for this specific parish were not found by this survey and may be held, if they survive at all, only at the Štátny oblastný archív (State Regional Archive) in Levoča, named in the catalog note as the microfilming source for the originals.
- **Language:** Latin and Hungarian, per the catalog note.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Hungary's statewide civil registration began in 1895 (outside the window this survey could confirm with a fetched wiki page for this place — see Quirks; no Slovakia/Hungary Vital Records page could be retrieved in this run). Throughout the 1700s-1890s target period itself, church registers (above) are therefore the operative vital-record source, not civil registration.

### Census records
- No collections_search or volume_search results were returned for this place in this survey (see Quirks) — no census holdings for Kolonica specifically could be confirmed here.

### Probate, land, military, cemetery, newspaper and immigration records
- No tool result in this survey surfaced place-specific holdings for these record types for Kolonica; collections_search, volume_search and the wiki place pages all returned empty or generic content (see Quirks). Pursue these through the Štátny oblastný archív (Levoča) and general Hungarian/Slovak archival finding aids outside this tool set.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch Catalog/Library | Cirkevná matrika, 1824-1924 (koha:727653; films 1792766, 1792767) | Church baptisms/marriages/deaths 1824-1924 | Online image access via the collection link noted above; film 1793684 images specifically unavailable |

**Coverage of this survey:** Only one catalog hit was returned for this exact place (totalHits: 1); collections_search and volume_search returned zero matches, so broader indexed/digitized coverage for Kolonica could not be assessed in this run.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Štátny oblastný archív (State Regional Archive), Levoča | Original parish registers microfilmed for the FamilySearch catalog entry above | In-person or by written request (not detailed by any tool result in this survey) |

## Records NOT online
- Any 18th-century (pre-1824) Kolonica parish records, if they survive, were not located online by this survey; their existence and location are unconfirmed here.
- General civil, land, probate, and military records for this village were not surfaced by any tool in this survey.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey stated that any Kolonica record set was destroyed; the earliest confirmed register point is 1824, but this survey did not confirm whether earlier records never existed, were lost, or simply were not digitized/cataloged in the data this tool set reached.

## Research tips
- Search under both the modern name 'Kolonica, Snina, Slovakia' and the historical name 'Kolonica, Zemplén, Hungary' — the catalog entry itself uses both, and most of the 1700s-1890s period falls under the Hungarian administration.
- The register is in Latin and Hungarian — expect to need reading skill in both for the 1824-1924 run, per the FamilySearch Catalog note.
- Use the alternate online collection link named in the catalog note (familysearch.org/search/collection/1554443) rather than film 1793684, whose images the catalog marks unavailable.
- Because this survey's FamilySearch Wiki place-page and collection-search calls for this specific village returned no usable data, re-run or supplement this guide directly against FamilySearch's website and the Levoča regional archive before concluding no earlier records exist.

Here is what the locality guide found for **Berkshire County, Massachusetts, 1820–1850**, focused on births, marriages, and deaths:

---

## Vital Records (Civil/Town Level)

In Massachusetts, vital records have always been kept at the **town** (not county) level by the town clerk. Massachusetts introduced a **statewide recording system starting in 1841** — before that, only locally-kept town books exist. So for your 1820–1850 window:

- **1820–1840:** Town clerk records only (held by each individual town)
- **1841–1850:** Both town clerk records and the new state system
- Marriage intentions were typically recorded in the bride's home town (sometimes in the groom's as well)

---

## Digitized Holdings Found

Two image volumes were found — both are **browse-only** (no name index; you must flip through images page-by-page):

1. **"Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," Berkshire, Massachusetts, 1761–1850** — 512 images (FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 004500891)
2. **Pittsfield Congregational Church Records, 1791–1850** — 274 images (FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 004500892)

Additionally, two **statewide indexed collections** on FamilySearch should include Berkshire County towns:

- **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (collection 2061550)
- **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (collection 1921657)

---

## Cross-Border Consideration

Because your family's town sits near both the **New York** and **Vermont** lines, you should also search the adjoining counties in those states. Check a map for which specific New York (likely Columbia or Rensselaer) and Vermont (likely Bennington) counties border the town and run the same kind of records search there.

---

## Other Repositories

General-purpose external repositories that may hold relevant records include FindAGrave (cemetery records), Newspapers.com (historical papers), Ancestry, and NARA/Fold3 (census and federal records).

---

If you'd like, the next step would be building a research plan — ordering which of these volumes and collections to search first and in what sequence.

**Vital records (civil/town level).** The FamilySearch Wiki page "Massachusetts Vital Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records) states that in Massachusetts, vital records have always originated at the **town** level (not the county), kept by the town or city clerk. Massachusetts was the first state to begin a unified **statewide** recording system, starting in **1841** — but the city of Boston is specifically excluded from that statewide system until **1850**; nothing in that page suggests other towns, including those in Berkshire County, were excluded. So for your 1820–1850 window: before 1841, the only vital records are the town's own locally-kept books; from 1841 the state system picks them up too (originals still held by the town clerk). Marriage intentions were typically recorded in the bride's home town, with a second recording possibly made in the groom's town.

**Digitized holdings found.** `volume_search` returned two digitized, browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) image volumes for Berkshire County in this window: imageGroupNumber 004500891, "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," covering Berkshire, Massachusetts generally, 1761–1850 (512 images); and imageGroupNumber 004500892, Congregational church records for **Pittsfield**, Berkshire County, 1791–1850 (274 images). Both must be browsed image-by-image; there is no name index into either. `collections_search` (run at the Massachusetts state level, since FamilySearch collections are organized statewide for the US) also surfaced "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection 2061550) and "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection 1921657) as statewide indexed collections that should include Berkshire towns.

**Gaps and caveats, stated plainly.** `catalog_search` returned zero hits at both the Berkshire County level and the Massachusetts state level — a cataloging gap in this tool, not evidence the records don't exist (the town-clerk and church volumes above prove they do). `place_population` returned no data for Berkshire County in this run, so no population figures can be reported. The four required FamilySearch Wiki "place page" sections (home/getting-started/online-records/research-tips) all returned only generic boilerplate content with no Berkshire- or Massachusetts-specific facts, so none of their specifics can be cited; the same was true of the constructed-URL pages for a Berkshire County genealogy page, Massachusetts Church Records, and Massachusetts Naming Customs — each redirected to a generic "Genealogy Records" template rather than a jurisdiction-specific page. That means I have no tool-sourced data on Berkshire's neighboring counties, Massachusetts naming customs, or confirmed Congregational/other-denomination founding dates beyond what the Pittsfield volume itself shows (1791 start).

**Cross-border instruction.** Because your family's town sits near both the New York and Vermont lines, you should search the adjoining New York and Vermont counties' town/church vital records as well — this survey did not confirm which specific counties border your town (the Neighboring Counties data did not come back), so check a map and run the same kind of search for each adjoining county by name.

**External repositories.** `external_links_search` returned (at the Massachusetts/generic level, not Berkshire-specific) FindAGrave for cemetery records, Newspapers.com for historical papers, and NARA/Ancestry/Fold3 for census, military, and other federal records — useful but general-purpose, not place-curated for Berkshire specifically.

---
This survey covered Berkshire County, Massachusetts for 1820 to 1850, focused on birth, marriage, and death records; in Massachusetts those records have always been kept by the individual town, not the county, with a statewide collection system added in 1841, and two old scanned volumes were found covering the county generally and the town of Pittsfield's Congregational church, but both are plain picture scans you'd have to flip through page by page since neither has a name search; several of the usual background pages that would normally name neighboring towns or explain church record history came back empty or generic in this search, so a few details (exact neighboring counties, other towns' church records) still need to be checked by hand, and because the family's town sits right on the New York and Vermont borders, records on both those sides should be searched too. Next, if you'd like, I can build a research plan that lays out which of these volumes and collections to search first and in what order.

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** 1761, carved from Hampshire County

---

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**How it worked:** Massachusetts vital records were kept by each **town/city clerk**, not the county. The state began a permanent statewide registration system in **1841** (Boston excluded until 1850), so:
- **1820–1840:** Rely on town-level registers and church records
- **1841–1850:** Both town registers and the statewide series apply

**Marriage intentions** may be recorded in the bride's town, the groom's town, *and* their town of residence — search all three.

**What's online:**
| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 | 2061550 | 3.4M+ records; free |
| Berkshire town clerk vital/town records, 1761–1850 | Image group 004500891 (512 images) | **0% indexed — browse only, no name search** |

**Published compilations:** "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" books exist for 200+ Massachusetts towns — once you identify the specific town, check for one of these.

---

## Church Records

- **Denominations confirmed:** Congregational (present in Pittsfield with records from 1791)
- **What's online:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (id 1921657, ~987K records)
- **Berkshire-specific digitized volume:** Image group 004500892 — Pittsfield Congregational church records, 1791–1850 (274 images); **0% indexed — browse only**
- Other denominations in the county were not surfaced by this survey; check locally.

---

| Naturalization | Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (id 1459213) | Covers 1820–1850 |

| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal originals (military, naturalization) | Free/in-person |

1. **Identify the specific town first.** Records are filed at the town level, not the county. Once you know the town, the guide can be sharpened to that town's clerk, church records, and any published vital-records compilation.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840-1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811, per FamilySearch place data (dateRange +1811/). No parent jurisdiction or boundary detail could be confirmed: `place_search_all` returned no results for this place, and every FamilySearch Wiki place page fetched returned only generic template content (empty standardPlace/placeName in the response), not Schuylkill-specific text.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by tools this run.
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for Schuylkill, Pennsylvania for 1840-1880.
- **Economy / ethnic composition / religious denominations:** Not confirmed by tools this run beyond what the collections below imply (an active, English- and German-speaking church-record-keeping population in the period).

## Boundary changes
`place_search_all` returned no jurisdictional history for Schuylkill County, so no boundary change could be confirmed or ruled out by tools this run. Treat this as an open gap, not a statement of stability.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not confirmed. The `Pennsylvania_Vital_Records` wiki fetch returned only generic template content (no Schuylkill- or Pennsylvania-specific registration start date or level), so no civil-registration date can be stated from this survey.
- **What exists:** A Marriage Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936753) covering 1870-1910 was found via `volume_search`, 94 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable -- browse-only.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds the digitized images; no physical custodian was confirmed by tools this run.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death civil-registration volume was returned for 1840-1880.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** The Church Records volume below (1842-1895) is the main alternative for this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Not named by any tool result this run.
- **Record types:** A Church Records volume (007936751), 1842-1895, 187 images, English and German, 0% indexed and not full-text searchable -- must be browsed image by image, and German-language entries require a German reader.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized image group 007936751.
- **Gaps:** No denomination-specific coverage or loss could be confirmed; a separate collection, "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)" (collections_search id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH), covers 1708-1985 with 1,245,830 records and 982,415 persons indexed.
- **Language:** English and German (image group 007936751).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Ancestry's curated external link "1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) covers the county for 1850.
- **State/provincial census:** None found by tools this run.
- **Access:** The 1850 federal census is on Ancestry per the link above; FamilySearch-indexed coverage for this county's census years was not separately confirmed this run.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** A Probate Records volume (007936749), 1851-1930, 412 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable -- browse-only. Also "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collections_search id 1999196), recordCount and personCount both 0 (an unindexed image-only collection by this tool's count).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized images; courthouse of origin not confirmed this run.

### Land records
- **Types:** A Deed Records volume (007936752), 1815-1900, 543 images, 22% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized images (image group 007936752); recorder of deeds office not confirmed this run.

### Military records
- Not confirmed by tools this run; no volume or collection surfaced a military record type for this place/period.

### Naturalization / immigration records
- A Naturalization Records volume (007936750), 1849-1915, 298 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable -- browse-only.
- Ancestry's curated link "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" predates the period and is listed for completeness, not as a period source.

### Tax records
- The Ancestry curated link above (Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801) predates 1840-1880 and is background only; no in-period tax collection was returned.

### Other record types
- None confirmed by tools this run.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (church records, 1708-1985, 1,245,830 records); 1999196 (Probate Records, 1683-1994); image groups 007936749-007936753 (Probate, Naturalization, Church, Deed, Marriage) | Browse-only church/probate/naturalization/marriage coverage for 1840-1880 | Free |
| Ancestry | "1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) | 1850 federal census | Subscription |
| Ancestry | "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) | Pre-period tax background only | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 5 total matching volumes and the summary marked the result set complete (`complete: true`), so all 5 were examined; no further pages exist to fetch.

### Physical repositories
- Not confirmed by tools this run: `catalog_search` returned `totalHits: 0` for Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, which is a cataloguing gap, not evidence that no physical holdings exist.

## Records NOT online
No civil birth or death registers for 1840-1880 were returned by any tool this run; if they exist, they were not confirmed as digitized.

## Known record losses
No record loss was stated by any tool result this run; absence of an online hit is reported as a coverage gap, not a loss.

## Research tips
- Every FamilySearch Wiki page fetched for this place and for Pennsylvania (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips, and the Pennsylvania_Vital_Records page) returned only generic template content with no place-specific facts -- do not rely on any date or record claim appearing to come from them.
- Browse image-by-image for the five unindexed/low-indexed volumes (Probate, Naturalization, Church, Deed at 22%, Marriage); only the Deed Records volume has any name index.
- The Church Records volume (1842-1895) includes German-language entries -- a German reader is needed for full coverage.
- `catalog_search` and `place_population` both returned empty for this place; re-run this survey later, or supplement with a direct FamilySearch Wiki visit, since these gaps may reflect a tool/data limitation rather than true absence.
- Use the Ancestry 1850 federal census link directly for that census year; no FamilySearch-specific census collection was confirmed this run.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

**Standard place used:** Billy, County Antrim, Ireland (pre-1922 jurisdiction); modern equivalent "Billy, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom."

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Location:** Barony of Carey (partly) and chiefly Lower Dunluce, Poor Law Union of Coleraine, County Antrim, Province of Ulster. Contains the post town of Bushmills and part of Dunserverick.
- **Ecclesiastical history:** Billy was formerly head of an ecclesiastical union comprising Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, together forming the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor; the rectory/vicarage of Billy alone now constitutes the archdeaconry.
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (parish forms part of the district of Coleraine), Presbyterian, Covenanter, and Wesleyan Methodist meeting houses.

---

## Boundary Changes

Ireland's 1922 partition split jurisdiction of national record-keeping: County Antrim remained in Northern Ireland. Records up to 1922 may appear filed under "County Antrim, Ireland" or "County Antrim, Northern Ireland" labels; they are now split administratively between PRONI (Northern Ireland) and the NAI/GRO (Republic), though copies of many national-level records up to 1922 exist in both. No sub-parish boundary change during 1780–1870 itself was found.

---

## Church Records — The Core Gap

The Billy civil parish's own FamilySearch Wiki page has **no content under its Catholic / Church of Ireland / Presbyterian / Methodist / Society of Friends / Others subheadings** — it only points to the general Ireland Church Records article. This is a cataloguing gap, not evidence the registers don't exist.

| Denomination | National context | Billy-specific start date |
|---|---|---|
| Church of Ireland | Registers began 1536; ~two-thirds destroyed in 1922 PRO Dublin fire | Not found in tools |
| Catholic | Most rural parishes from mid-1700s; most post-1828 (Emancipation) | Not found in tools |
| Presbyterian | As early as 1600s; average start date ~1830 | Not found in tools |
| Methodist / Covenanter | Meeting houses known in parish | Not found in tools |

**Treat the national averages above as context only — confirm surviving registers directly with the repositories below.**

---

## Repositories and Online Indexes to Close Coverage Gaps

| Repository / Index | What it covers | Address / URL | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)** | Holds originals and microfilm for Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Catholic, and Methodist parish registers for County Antrim; its *Guide to Church Records* identifies what churches existed per parish and what survives | 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast BT3 9HQ. Tel: 028 9053 4800. Email: proni@communities-ni.gov.uk. # Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

**Standard place used:** Billy, County Antrim, Ireland (pre-1922 jurisdiction); modern equivalent "Billy, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom."

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Location:** Barony of Carey (partly) and chiefly Lower Dunluce, Poor Law Union of Coleraine, County Antrim, Province of Ulster. Contains the post town of Bushmills and part of Dunserverick. (FamilySearch Wiki, [Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Ecclesiastical history:** Billy was formerly head of an ecclesiastical union also comprising Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, together forming the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor; the rectory/vicarage of Billy alone now constitutes the archdeaconry (same source).
- **Religious denominations present:** Roman Catholic (parish forms part of the district of Coleraine), Presbyterian, Covenanter, and Wesleyan Methodist meeting houses (same source). No population figures, census-count data, or economy/ethnic-composition detail were returned by any tool for this specific parish — `place_population` returned no data for either "Antrim, Ireland" or "Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom," so this guide does not state any.

## Boundary changes
Ireland's 1922 partition split jurisdiction of national record-keeping: County Antrim stayed in Northern Ireland. Records up to 1922 may appear filed under either "County Antrim, Ireland" or "County Antrim, Northern Ireland" labels, and are now split administratively between the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI) for Northern Ireland and the National Archives of Ireland (NAI)/General Register Office (GRO) for the Republic — though copies of many national-level records up to 1922 exist in both repositories (FamilySearch Wiki, [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)). No sub-parish boundary change during 1780–1870 itself was found in the retrieved sources.

## Available record types

### Church records (the focus of this request)
The Billy civil parish's own FamilySearch Wiki page has **no content under any of its Catholic / Church of Ireland / Presbyterian / Methodist / Society of Friends / Others subheadings** — it only points to the general Ireland Church Records article. This is a genuine gap in this survey's data for Billy specifically, not evidence the registers don't exist.

- **Church of Ireland:** General Ireland-wide registers began in 1536, but roughly two-thirds were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office (Dublin) fire. No start date specific to Billy parish's own Church of Ireland registers was found. (Ireland Church Records page, above)
- **Catholic:** Nationally, Catholic registers mostly begin from the mid-1700s, but most rural parishes did not start keeping registers until after Catholic Emancipation (1828); city registers can run from the 1750s. No Billy-specific start date was found.
- **Presbyterian:** Nationally, registers date as far back as the 1600s in places, but the average starting date is 1830. No Billy-specific start date was found.
- **Methodist / Covenanter:** Known to have meeting houses in the parish (per the parish page), but no register dates were returned for either.
- **Gaps:** Because no denomination-specific start dates, surviving-register details, or losses were returned for Billy itself, treat all of the above national averages as context only, not as fact about Billy's registers — confirm directly with the repositories below.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Birth and death registration began nationally in 1864 (level not further specified beyond "government registration" in the Billy parish page). Protestant marriage registration began in 1845, with registration of all marriages by 1864. (Billy Civil Parish page, above) This predates most of the 1780–1870 window, so for the bulk of the target period church registers are the primary vital-event source.
- **Where held:** General Register Office (Republic) / GRONI (Northern Ireland) post-1922 split, per the Ireland Church Records background note.

### Census records
No census collections, volumes, or population data were returned for this parish or County Antrim by any tool in this survey (`place_population`, `collections_search`, and `volume_search` all returned empty results for "Antrim, Ireland" and "Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom"). The FamilySearch Wiki's Billy page points only to the general [Ireland Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Census) article, which this survey did not fetch. Note nationally that most 19th-century Irish censuses before 1901 were destroyed; tithe applotment books and Griffith's Valuation (below) are the standard substitutes.

### Probate and court records
The Billy parish page points to [Ireland Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Probate_Records) for detail, which this survey did not fetch; no specifics for Billy were returned.

### Land and tax records
- Griffith's Valuation (property valuation for tax) began in the 1840s under Richard Griffith; Tithe Applotment records (a tax paid to the church) began in the 1820s. (Billy Civil Parish page) These are standard substitutes for missing census years.

### Other record types
School records are referenced only by a pointer to the general [Ireland Schools and Education](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Schools_and_Education) article; no Billy-specific content was returned.

## Known record losses
Nationally, roughly two-thirds of Church of Ireland registers were destroyed, and the 1922 Public Record Office of Dublin fire destroyed large classes of probate, marriage-bond, and other records — the Betham, Crossle, and Thrift genealogical abstracts noted above exist specifically as substitutes for that loss. (Ireland Church Records page) No tool result stated that Billy parish's own registers specifically were lost or destroyed; absence of listed registers on its Wiki page is a cataloguing/content gap in that page, not confirmation of loss.

## Coverage of this survey
`collections_search`, `volume_search`, `catalog_search`, and `place_population` returned no results for any Antrim-level standardPlace tried in this session — a genuine coverage/indexing gap in those tools for this place rather than a statement that no digitized collections exist. The three generic `wiki_place_page` sections for Northern Ireland (getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only boilerplate generic content, not place-specific pages, so this guide draws its research-tips content from the Ireland Church Records article instead. The Billy civil parish page itself (home section) was found but is substantially empty under Church Records.

## Research tips
- Search all denominations' registers for the area, including Church of Ireland registers, even if the family is believed non-Anglican. (Ireland Church Records page)
- Search surrounding civil parishes if records aren't found in Billy itself — Catholic parish boundaries differed from civil-parish/Church of Ireland boundaries. (same)
- Use the PRONI "Guide to Church Records" PDF first to identify exactly which churches served Billy and where their surviving registers are physically held, since the Billy parish's own FamilySearch Wiki page does not list its registers.
- Because national civil registration only reaches back to 1845 (marriages) / 1864 (births, deaths), church registers and Griffith's Valuation/Tithe Applotment records are the primary sources for nearly the entire 1780–1870 window.

---
The survey covered Billy civil parish, near Bushmills in County Antrim, Northern Ireland, for the years 1780 to 1870, focusing on where old church baptism, marriage and burial books might be found; unfortunately the specific page for Billy parish on the main genealogy reference site turned out to be essentially blank under every church heading, so this guide instead draws on Ireland-wide guidance and points you to the record-holding offices themselves — chiefly the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland in Belfast and the Church of Ireland's own library in Dublin, both of which keep guides listing exactly which chapels' registers survive and where, plus a cluster of paid and free index websites (Ancestry, FindMyPast, the National Library of Ireland's Catholic register site, and FamilySearch) that can substitute where original registers are missing or were destroyed in a 1922 fire in Dublin. # Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840-1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 10, 1798, from Lincoln and Green counties (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)
- **County seat:** Somerset, Kentucky
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky, United States
- **Population during period:** Not returned by place_population in this survey (empty result) - a data gap, not a finding of no population.
- **Key historical events:** Record-destroying disasters in 1838 and 1871 at the courthouse.

## Boundary changes
No boundary changes to Pulaski County itself were found within 1840-1880; the county has existed in its formed jurisdiction since 1798 per place_search_all.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level 1852-1862 and 1874-1878 (poor compliance); statewide registration 1911, general compliance ~1917 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records). Marriage was recorded from county formation (1799) onward, per the county page.
- **What exists:** Per the Pulaski County Genealogy page, birth records from 1852, marriage from 1799, death from 1852.
- **Where held:** County-level originals at Pulaski County Courthouse; pre-1911 copies microfilmed at KDLA.
- **Gaps:** 1838 and 1871 disasters; the 1862-1874 and 1878-1892 lapses in the state registration law.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, marriage bonds (1799-1871, digitized on FamilySearch per the county page).

### Church records
- Denominations and record types not detailed by any tool result in this survey - a coverage gap. The Pulaski County Historical Society is named by the FamilySearch Wiki as holding "the most comprehensive collection of church records and obituaries from local newspapers."

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Earliest county record date given as 1810 by the FamilySearch Wiki county page; the 1840-1880 federal censuses (1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) fall within normal national coverage, though this survey did not pull specific collection IDs (collections_search returned zero results for this place).
- **Access:** Not resolved in this survey - collections_search and volume_search both returned zero matches for Pulaski, Kentucky; treat as a digitization gap, confirm directly on FamilySearch/Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, court orders, per the county page.
- **Date range:** From 1801 (probate) and 1799 (court), per the county page; will books 1801-1929 are digitized on FamilySearch.
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street, #208, Somerset, KY 42502); microfilmed copies at KDLA.
- **Gaps:** 1838 and 1871 disasters noted by the Wiki page may have affected these series; extent not detailed by any tool result.

### Land records
- **Types:** Deeds, per the county page.
- **Date range:** From 1799 (county formation).
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse; microfilmed at KDLA.

### Military records
- Not detailed by any tool result for this county in this survey - a coverage gap. The Civil War (1861-1865) falls within the target period; service, pension, and draft records for Kentucky Union/Confederate units would be at NARA and the Kentucky adjutant general's records, per general FamilySearch guidance, but no Pulaski-specific collection was returned.

### Cemetery records
- Not detailed by a Pulaski-specific tool result. Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is listed among the county's curated external links by external_links_search.

### Newspaper records
- Not detailed by a Pulaski-specific tool result. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is listed among the county's curated external links by external_links_search. The Historical Society is also named as holding obituary collections from local newspapers.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not a coastal/port county; naturalization records, if any, would be filed in county or federal court and were not detailed by a tool result in this survey.

### Tax records
- Not detailed by a Pulaski-specific tool result in this survey - a coverage gap; Ancestry's curated collections for the county (per external_links_search) include county tax lists.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Mississippi Territory (Alabama Portion), ca. 1798–1817

## Jurisdiction Overview
Your ancestor in what is now Alabama around 1800 would have lived under the **U.S. Mississippi Territory**, not an Alabama state government — Alabama didn't become a state until 1819. The territory was established in 1798, and present-day Alabama was split off as a separate Alabama Territory in 1817, then admitted to statehood in 1819.

The earliest county covering most of the Alabama portion was **Washington County (est. 1800)**. It subdivided rapidly:
- **Madison County** (1808) — northern Alabama
- **Baldwin County** (1809) — coastal/southern Alabama
- **Mobile County** (1812) — Mobile Bay area

**Research tip:** Always search the parent county (Washington) first before its successor counties; your ancestor's earliest records will be filed there.

---

## Available Records

### Census Records
- **Federal census:** 1800 and 1810 schedules nominally covered this area, but survivorship is uncertain — verify directly with the state archives.
- **Territorial census enumerations** were taken in **1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816**, held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery) and the Mississippi Department of Archives and History (Jackson).
- FamilySearch collection: *Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890* (collection 1927171)

### Land Records
Federal land sales through the St. Stephens and Huntsville land offices began **1803**. These are among the richest records for this period:
- **National Archives**, Record Group 49 (land entry files)
- **BLM General Land Office** website (online, indexed)
- FamilySearch collection: *Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907* (collection 1919694, ~156,225 images)

### Court & Probate Records
Wills, inventories, administrations, guardianships — filed at the county level:
- FamilySearch collection: *Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920* (collection 1855293, ~122,835 images)
- County courthouses and/or state archives for original records

### Church Records
No civil vital registration (births, marriages, deaths) existed yet. Church registers are the primary substitute, though specific congregation survival rates were not confirmed in this survey.
- FamilySearch collection: *Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950* (collection 2034891)

### Military Records
The **Creek War (1813–1814)** falls near this period. Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants are held at the **National Archives (NARA)**. Militia rolls for the territorial period may be at the state archives.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History** (Montgomery) | Territorial census, county records for the Alabama portion | In-person / written request |
| **Mississippi Dept. of Archives & History** (Jackson) | Territorial census, territorial government records | In-person / written request |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Land entry files (RG 49), federal military records | In-person / online finding aids |
| **FamilySearch** (online) | Land, court, church, census substitute collections | Free |
| **BLM GLO website** | Federal land patents indexed | Free, online |
| **Fold3** | Military service/pension records | Subscription |

---

## Important Gaps to Know
- **No civil vital registration** existed in this period — there were no birth, marriage, or death record offices. Prioritize land, court/probate, and territorial census records.
- Territorial census enumerations (1801–1816) are **not confirmed as digitized** — contact the state archives in Montgomery or Jackson directly.
- The FamilySearch catalog returned limited hits for the "Mississippi Territory" standardPlace — search under **"Mississippi, United States"** and **"Alabama, United States"** in the FamilySearch Catalog for broader results.

---

## Suggested Starting Points
1. **Land entry files** (BLM GLO / NARA RG 49) — common first record for settlers
2. **Washington County court and probate records** — earliest county covering nearly all of Alabama
3. **Territorial census enumerations** at the Alabama or Mississippi state archives
4. **FamilySearch collections** listed above for digitized/indexed material

# Locality Guide: Mississippi Territory (Alabama portion), United States (ca. 1798–1817)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1798 by the U.S. Congress from land ceded by Georgia and South Carolina (disputed with Spain until 1813 for the lower portion); present-day Alabama was carved off as the separate Alabama Territory in 1817, then admitted as a state in 1819 (confirmed by `place_search`: "Alabama, United States" dateRange begins 1819; "Mississippi Territory, United States" dateRange is 1798–1817).
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single center — territorial government sat at Natchez, then Washington, Mississippi; the Alabama portion's earliest county, Washington County (est. 1800), covered most of present-day Alabama (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Mississippi Territory Genealogy," County Formation section).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (federal territory, no state-level government in this period).
- **Population during period:** This survey could not retrieve population figures — `place_population` returned no data for "Mississippi Territory, United States."
- **Economy/ethnic composition:** Not covered by the tool results retrieved in this survey; for historical background beyond what directly shapes records, consult the historical-context skill.
- **Key historical events:** The Creek War (1813–1814) and subsequent land cessions opened much of central/south Alabama to settlement and drove the 1817–1819 territorial/statehood transition (Wikipedia, "Alabama").

## Boundary changes
County formation in the Mississippi Territory began with Adams and Pickering counties in 1799; Washington County (1800) covered most of present-day Alabama. As settlement expanded, counties subdivided rapidly: Baldwin (1809), Madison (1808), and Mobile (1812) were carved from the Alabama portion (FamilySearch Wiki, "Mississippi Territory Genealogy," County Formation). **This is a continuous record trail, not separate record sets:** an ancestor in what became, say, Madison or Baldwin County before 1808/1809 will have earlier records filed under Washington County — search the parent county first, then the subdivided county, for the same family.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No territorial or county civil vital registration existed in this period; this survey found no wiki page stating an Alabama/Mississippi civil registration start date for births, marriages, or deaths this early (Alabama's statewide system came much later, well after 1819, and is outside this period).
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds/licenses were recorded at the county level (Washington County and its successors) as part of court records, not as separate "vital records."
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers and county court/marriage bond books are the primary substitutes.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Not confirmed by tool results in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, where congregations existed, likely predating any civil system.
- **Gaps:** This survey did not confirm specific congregations, dates, or surviving registers for this place; FamilySearch's generic guidance notes church registers "often predate civil registration by decades" and recommends checking both parish and denominational archives (FamilySearch Wiki, "Genealogy Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records).

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1800 and 1810 federal censuses nominally covered Mississippi Territory, but no federal census schedules survive for the Alabama portion before 1820 (this is a widely known loss, but this survey's tool results did not themselves state it — treat as unconfirmed by this run and verify directly).
- **Territorial census:** A wiki_search result states territorial census enumerations were taken in 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816, held at the Mississippi Department of Archives and History (Jackson) and the Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery) (FamilySearch Wiki, "Mississippi Territory Genealogy," Territorial Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region under Spanish Control (1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The Arkansas region (centered on Arkansas Post, the first permanent European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley, founded 1686) passed from French Louisiana to Spanish control via the 1763 Treaty of Paris. Spain administered the territory until 1800, when it was secretly retroceded to France, then sold to the United States in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary civil-registration substitute)*
Since there was no Spanish civil-registration system, births, marriages, and burials were recorded by the **Roman Catholic Church** — the only organized denomination at Arkansas Post.

**One confirmed digitized source was found:**
- **Image group 008814402** — *Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, 1763–1800*, 64 images, in **Spanish**
- **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image by image, page by page, in Spanish-language handwriting

### Census Records (*Padrones*)
Spanish colonial censuses (padrones) were reportedly kept at Arkansas Post, but **no digitized or indexed collection for them was found** on FamilySearch. Their existence is referenced in a FamilySearch Wiki search snippet but was not independently confirmed.

### Land Records
Spanish crown land concessions were granted by the local administration at Arkansas Post. Per a FamilySearch Wiki search snippet (unverified by direct page load), surviving records are reportedly held at:
- Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock
- **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain (original colonial administrative and land records)
- Library of Congress (some material on microfilm)

### Military Records
Arkansas Post was a Spanish military garrison. Post/garrison registers (troop rosters, correspondence) likely exist, but **no specific collection or volume** was found by this survey's tools.

### Probate & Court Records
Spanish colonial civil and military administrative records likely included judicial papers, but nothing specific was located in any indexed collection.

---

## FamilySearch Collections for Arkansas

`collections_search` returned only three indexed Arkansas collections — **none reaching before 1819**:

| Collection | Dates |
|---|---|
| Arkansas, County Marriages, 1837–1957 | 1837–1957 |
| Arkansas, Freedmen's Bureau Field Office Records, 1865–1872 | 1865–1872 |
| Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870 | 1819–1870 |

Do not expect name-searchable records for 1763–1800 through FamilySearch's main search interface.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (image group 008814402) | Spanish colonial sacramental registers, Arkansas Post, 1763–1800 | Free; browse-only, no name index |

### Physical Repositories *(leads to verify directly)*
| Repository | Reported Holdings |
|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock | Spanish colonial land concessions; transcribed sacramental registers |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial administrative and land records for Louisiana/Arkansas territory |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original or retained sacramental registers from Arkansas Post |
| Library of Congress | Microfilm copies of some colonial-era material |

> ⚠️ These repository names came from a FamilySearch Wiki search snippet. The underlying Wiki page did not fully load as Arkansas-specific content during this survey, so **verify directly** with each institution before relying on these leads.

---

## Records NOT Online

Spanish colonial land grants, civil/military administrative papers, and census (padron) records for Arkansas Post are **not found in any indexed FamilySearch collection**. Only the one browse-only sacramental register image set (1763–1800) is confirmed online.

---

## Known Record Losses

No tool result confirmed that Spanish colonial records were destroyed or lost. Their whereabouts are split among Little Rock, Seville, and Washington D.C. — verify with those institutions.

---

## Research Tips

1. **The only confirmed digitized resource** (image group 008814402) is in Spanish, not name-indexed, and must be browsed all 64 images by hand — plan for Spanish colonial handwriting/paleography.
2. **Contact directly:** Arkansas History Commission and the Diocese of Little Rock archives are your best first contacts for land and church records.
3. **For land grants:** The Archivo General de Indias in Seville holds original Spanish colonial administrative records for the Louisiana territory, including Arkansas.
4. **FamilySearch catalog** returned zero hits for Spanish colonial Arkansas — this is a digitization/cataloguing gap, not proof the records don't exist.
5. Because FamilySearch's indexed Arkansas collections only begin in 1819, plan on archival correspondence or a research trip rather than online name searches for this era.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region, under Spanish Control (1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The region around Arkansas Post was claimed by France (part of La Louisiane) from 1686, ceded to Spain by the 1763 Treaty of Paris, administered as Spanish Louisiana (Arkansas Post was the principal settlement) until Spain secretly retroceded Louisiana to France in 1800, and then passed to the United States in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase (Wikipedia: Arkansas, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas). FamilySearch's own place index only has a standardized "Arkansas, United States" record dated from 1836, so none of the place-level tools (population, wiki place pages) resolved a distinct Spanish-era jurisdiction — they returned only generic template content, not Arkansas-specific facts.
- **County seat/administrative center:** Arkansas Post, the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley, founded 1686 (Wikipedia).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Spanish Louisiana, 1763–1800 (then back to France, then the United States).
- **Population, economy, ethnic/religious composition during the period:** Not available from any tool in this survey — `place_population` returned no data for "Arkansas, United States," and the FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned only generic, non-jurisdiction-specific guidance, not Arkansas figures. Treat population and demographic detail here as unconfirmed.
- **Key historical events:** French settlement 1686; Spanish administration 1763–1800; secret retrocession to France 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803 (Wikipedia: Arkansas).

## Boundary changes
Before 1763 the post was under French colonial administration; from 1763 to 1800 under Spain; in 1800 it reverted to France; in 1803 it passed to the United States. This is a clean temporal succession (not a geographic split), so records from a given year will be filed under whichever power held the post at that date — Spanish-era material should be sought as "Spanish colonial Arkansas Post" records, not under any later Arkansas county filing scheme, since the county system was not created until decades afterward.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
There was no Spanish or later U.S. civil-registration system for this area in this period — civil-style vital events were recorded through the Catholic Church (see Church records) and, for military personnel, through post/garrison registers. No FamilySearch Wiki page specific to Spanish-era Arkansas registration start dates was retrievable in this survey — the per-jurisdiction Vital Records page could not be confirmed as Arkansas-specific (see Repository guide note).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (the only organized church at Spanish Arkansas Post).
- **Record types:** A `volume_search` of "Arkansas, United States" for 1686–1800 returned exactly one matching digitized volume: image group **008814402**, 64 images, covering "Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)" at Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, Arkansas, United States, dated **1763–1800**, in **Spanish**. It is **0% name-indexed** (`recordSearchablePercent: 0`) and **not full-text searchable** (`fulltextSearchable: false`) — it must be browsed image by image, with no name search, and read in Spanish.
- **Where held:** A `wiki_search` result (not independently verified by `wiki_read`, since the underlying page did not resolve to Arkansas-specific content) states that surviving French/Spanish-era sacramental registers from Arkansas Post are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, with transcriptions at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Arkansas Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records). Treat this as a lead to verify directly, not a confirmed citation, since the full page itself would not load as Arkansas-specific content when fetched.
- **Language:** Spanish (and likely some French-era entries pre-1763).
- **Gaps:** Full extent of surviving registers for 1763–1800 is not confirmed beyond the single 64-image volume found; `catalog_search` for "Arkansas, United States" and for "United States" with Arkansas Post/Spanish colonial keywords both returned **zero hits** — a cataloguing gap, not evidence the records don't exist.

### Census records
A `wiki_search` result references Spanish colonial censuses ("padrones") kept at Arkansas Post alongside civil and military records (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Arkansas Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). No volume or collection for these padrones was found by `volume_search` or `collections_search` in this survey — their digitization status is unconfirmed. `collections_search` for Arkansas returned only three collections, none earlier than 1819 (see Repository guide), so no Spanish-era census material is indexed on FamilySearch today.

### Probate and court records
Spanish colonial administration kept civil and military records at the post (same wiki_search result above), which would include land-grant and administrative/judicial paperwork, but no specific probate or court series for this period was located by any tool call — report this as unconfirmed rather than absent.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish colonial land concessions were granted by the Spanish crown's local administration at Arkansas Post (wiki_search result, "Arkansas Genealogy").
- **Where held:** The same source states Spanish colonial land-grant and related administrative records are held at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain, with some material on microfilm at the Library of Congress. These are the only repository names this survey could produce for this record type; they were not independently confirmed via `wiki_read` or `catalog_search` (both of which returned no Arkansas-specific or hit results), so verify directly before relying on them.

### Military records
Arkansas Post was a Spanish military garrison; post/garrison records (troop rosters, correspondence) likely exist but no specific collection, volume, or catalog entry was found by this survey's tools.

### Cemetery, newspaper, immigration, tax, and other records
No tool result in this survey returned anything specific to Spanish colonial Arkansas for these categories. Given the tiny, frontier-garrison nature of the settlement in this period, formal series of this kind (local newspapers, formal tax rolls, organized cemeteries with surviving sexton books) are unlikely to have existed in a form distinct from the church and military administrative records already noted; this survey did not confirm any digitized or physical holdings specific to them.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image group 008814402 — Spanish colonial sacramental registers, Arkansas Post, 1763–1800, browse-only, Spanish-language | Only confirmed digitized church-record source for the period | Free, browse-only (no name index) |

`collections_search` for "Arkansas, United States" returned only three indexed collections, none reaching back before 1819: "Arkansas, County Marriages, 1837-1957" (collection 1920452), "Arkansas, Freedmen's Bureau Field Office Records, 1865-1872" (collection 1713980), and "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870" (collection 2085124). None of these cover the 1763–1800 Spanish period; they are listed only to show what FamilySearch does and does not have indexed for Arkansas broadly.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Ohio (pre-statehood, c.1788–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview
Ohio became a state in **1803**. Before that, it was part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. The first county organized was **Washington County (1788)**, followed by **Hamilton County (1790)**. County boundaries shifted frequently throughout this period — a critical point for record research.

---

## Boundary Changes
- Before 1788: unorganized Northwest Territory with no county government.
- 1788: Washington County organized (the first county).
- 1790: Hamilton County organized.
- Boundary splits continued right up to statehood in 1803.

**Key tip:** Researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event — there is no single clean date rule. The FamilySearch Wiki states this explicitly.

Additionally, two distinct **land-grant districts** operated internally:
- **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) — metes-and-bounds survey, reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio) — grid survey.

Each district has a different record repository (see Land Records below).

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records
- **Civil registration** did not exist in this era. No statewide or county-level civil registration for this window was confirmed.
- **Substitute:** Use **church records** (collection 2246917 on FamilySearch — "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950") as the primary source for births, marriages, and deaths. This collection starts in 1787 and covers the full pre-statehood window.
- **Marriage records:** "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (collection 1803785) overlaps from 1789.
- **Death records:** The earliest death collection found ("Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001") does not reach back to this era — this is a confirmed documentation gap.

### Census Records
- Ohio was not separately enumerated in the 1790 federal census as a state.
- **Substitute:** "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850" (collection 1987542 on FamilySearch) functions as a census substitute for the 1800–1803 window.

### Land Records
- "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (collection 1542187 on FamilySearch) covers the full pre-statehood window online.
- **Virginia Military District warrants:** held at the **Virginia State Library**.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve records:** held at the **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland**.
- Two digitized volumes were also found:
  - *Territorial Land Records, Northwest Territory, 1788–1799* (image group 005112233) — 51 images, 0% indexed, browse-only.
  - *County Tax Records, Washington County, 1799–1803* (image group 005112240) — 73 images, 12% indexed.

### Probate & Court Records
- No online collection or catalog entry was returned for this era. These records likely survive on paper at **county courthouses** and the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus, but were not found digitized.

### Military Records
- No Ohio-specific military collection was surfaced. NARA holds federal-level service, pension, and bounty-land records for this era.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church records (1787–), marriages (1789–), land (1787–), tax records (1800–) | Free, online |
| **Virginia State Library** | Virginia Military District land warrants | In-person / written request |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland)** | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person |
| **Ohio History Connection (Columbus)** | Early territorial court and land records | In-person |
| **County courthouses** (Washington, Hamilton, etc.) | Probate, deeds, court records | In-person / mail |
| **NARA** | Federal military, pension, bounty-land | Online request / in-person |
| **Ancestry, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3** | Supplemental (census, cemetery, newspaper, military) | Subscription |

---

## Practical Research Tips

1. **Determine the county first.** Pin down which county — Washington (from 1788), Hamilton (from 1790), or a later split — governed your ancestor's location on the date of the event before searching any county-level record set.

2. **Identify the land district.** Determine whether your ancestor's land fell in the Virginia Military District or the Connecticut Western Reserve, as this dictates which archive and survey system to use for land records.

3. **Use tax records as a census substitute.** The 1800–1850 Ohio tax records (collection 1987542) fill the gap left by missing federal census coverage for the territorial period.

4. **Lead with church records for vital events.** Since civil registration did not exist, church registers (collection 2246917, from 1787) are the main substitute for births, marriages, and deaths.

5. **Go to physical repositories for court and probate.** No probate or court records from this era were found online — expect to contact the Ohio History Connection or relevant county courthouses directly.

---

*No project path was supplied, so this guide was not saved to a project research file. The two digitized FamilySearch volumes noted above are browse-only or minimally indexed — plan to read images directly for the territorial land records.*

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Statehood:** California entered the Union in **1850**, bypassing territorial status.
- **Population surge:** The Gold Rush, beginning January 1848 at Sutter's Mill (Coloma), brought roughly 300,000 migrants from across the US and abroad.
- **Record transition:** Pre-1850 records were created under Spanish/Mexican administration and mission authorities — a distinct series from the post-1850 American civil system.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (ID 2017276) — 789,456 records, indexed + images, covering county-level births from 1850.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Spanish/Mexican mission registers (1769–1834) record baptisms, marriages, and burials in Latin/Spanish.

### Church Records
- **Mission records:** "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" (FamilySearch collection ID 1804372) — 98,765 records, indexed + images. Franciscan mission registers, in Spanish, predating statehood.
- No Gold Rush-era Protestant church register collections were returned; treat as a coverage gap to verify independently.

### Census Records
- **Federal (1850):** The first federal census taken in California, but **some county returns were partially destroyed** — a known loss.
- **State substitute:** California State Census, 1850–1852 (FamilySearch image group 006601001) — 522 images, **88% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — a strong substitute for 1850 federal census gaps.

### Mining & Claim Records
- **Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849–1855** (FamilySearch image group 006601002) — 340 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**. Must be paged through manually.
- Held at county recorders' offices; also held by FamilySearch as digitized images.

### Immigration & Arrival Records
- **Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858** (FamilySearch image group 006601003) — 298 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**.
- **Ship passenger manifests** into San Francisco are held at the **National Archives, San Bruno facility**.
- Review full manifest pages for a family group, not just the head of household.

### Land Records
- Federal patents are held at the **BLM General Land Office**; deeds and grants at county courthouses.

### Probate & Court Records
- Wills, administrations, and guardianships at the county/district level. Naturalizations pre-1906 could be filed in any court of record — check county courts.

### Voter Registration (Post-Gold Rush)
- "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" (FamilySearch collection ID 1923340) — 1,345,678 records, indexed + images. Begins in **1866** (after the Gold Rush decade), so documents later residents — useful if the ancestor stayed in California.

### Newspapers & Cemetery Records
- **Newspapers.com** — general repository for historical California newspapers (verify specific title coverage directly).
- **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) — cemetery and memorial records.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | County Births 1850–1919; County Marriages 1850–1952; Mission Records 1769–1850; Great Registers 1866–1910; 1850–52 State Census; Mining Claim & Port Arrival volumes (browse-only) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| **NARA** | Ship passenger manifests (San Bruno facility) | In-person/request |
| **Fold3** | Military records | Subscription |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **County Recorders' Offices** | Mining claim registers, deeds, early births/marriages |
| **California State Archives** | State-level records, Great Registers originals |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Extensive Gold Rush manuscript collections — diaries, letters, mining company papers (largely unindexed) |
| **California State Library** | Gold Rush-era manuscripts |
| **NARA, San Bruno** | Original ship passenger manifests |

---

## Known Record Losses
- Some **1850 federal census county returns** for California are missing or destroyed. The **1850–1852 State Census** (image group 006601001, 88% indexed) is the documented substitute.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1850–1852 California State Census** to offset federal census losses — it's 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable.
2. **Browse mining claim registers and port arrival registers image-by-image** — both are digitized but carry no name index. Plan for manual page-by-page searching.
3. **The Bancroft Library and California State Library** hold substantial unindexed manuscript material (diaries, letters, mining company papers) that can place a specific migrant at a specific camp or company — worth a written inquiry.
4. **Great Registers begin in 1866**, so a Gold Rush migrant who left California before then won't appear there. Don't rule someone out for its absence.
5. **Narrow to the specific county or mining camp** as soon as possible — county-level records (deeds, probate, claim registers) are where most individual Gold Rush activity is actually documented.
6. The FamilySearch catalog search for "gold rush mining" in California returned zero hits during this survey — this appears to be a cataloguing gap, not evidence such records don't exist. Try narrower place/keyword combinations directly in the FamilySearch Catalog.

---

**Coverage note:** This survey covered the state of California as a whole for approximately 1848–1860. The richest Gold Rush manuscript material sits unindexed in the Bancroft Library and California State Library rather than online. Some FamilySearch Wiki pages for California-specific details returned only generic content and should be double-checked directly before relying on them for registration start dates or strategy claims.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s Colonial Period, c. 1700–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Origin:** Originally Dutch New Amsterdam (1626), seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York; by the 1700s it was the administrative and commercial capital of the Province of New York.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial administration) until 1783.
- **Key denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian churches — all kept extensive records.
- **Period ends:** American independence in 1783.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary substitute for vital registration)*
There was no civil birth/marriage/death registration during the colonial period — church records are the key source.

- **Dutch Reformed Church register** (1700–1776): FamilySearch image group **007733180** (211 images). **Browse-only, in Dutch, 0% name-indexed.** Must be read page by page.
- **Broad collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940" (FamilySearch collection **1469062**, ~2.3 million records/images) covers multiple denominations across the period.
- **Gaps noted:** No separate Anglican or Presbyterian volume was returned by the tools — this is a survey gap, not evidence those registers don't survive.

### Probate Records (Wills & Administrations)
- Wills proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** are indexed in the published *Abstracts of Wills* series (New-York Historical Society) — a key finding aid.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (id **1542780**).

### Land Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (id **2078654**).
- The **New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the New York State Archives also hold colonial-era land and administrative records.

### Tax Records
- "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804" (FamilySearch id **1678432**) falls just after this period but can serve as a cross-reference.

### Census / Enumeration
- The first U.S. federal census is 1790 — at the edge of this period. No colonial-era New York enumeration was returned by tools in this survey.

### Military Records
- Colonial militia rolls listing men of military age are known to survive for some years, but no online FamilySearch collection or catalog hit specific to this was returned — treat as archival-only pending further research.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Collection | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1640–1940 (1469062); Land Records (2078654); Probate Records (1542780); Dutch Reformed register vol. 007733180 | Free access; Dutch Reformed volume is browse-only in Dutch |
| **Find A Grave** | General coverage | Cemetery records |
| **Newspapers.com** | General coverage | Historical newspapers (subscription) |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | General coverage | Federal/military records |

### Physical / Archival
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **New York State Archives** | New York Colonial Manuscripts (land, administrative) |
| **New-York Historical Society** | *Abstracts of Wills* (published series); colonial collections |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** | Colonial-era collections |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with church records.** Since there was no civil registration, baptism, marriage, and burial registers are your primary vital record substitutes. The Dutch Reformed Church register (007733180) covers 1700–1776 but requires Dutch-language reading and manual image browsing.
2. **Use the *Abstracts of Wills* as a finding aid.** This published index to the Prerogative Court wills is an efficient entry point to probate records before diving into the raw FamilySearch collection.
3. **Check both the broad church records collection and the specific volume.** FamilySearch's "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940" may include other denominations' registers not separately indexed.
4. **For records not online** — militia rolls, Mayor's Court records, and the New York Colonial Manuscripts — plan a contact or visit to the New York State Archives or New-York Historical Society.
5. **Language note:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch through at least the mid-1700s; the translation agent can assist if you encounter period Dutch text.

---

The next logical step would be to build a research plan targeting the Dutch Reformed church register and the probate and land record collections identified here, then fill gaps through the physical repositories.
