# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview
Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies and contributed more troops to the Revolutionary War than any other colony. Major engagements, including the Siege of Yorktown (1781), occurred on Virginia soil. County-level record-keeping dating back to the 1630s gives Virginia one of the best-documented colonial record bases in British North America — the county court, not any state civil registry, is the primary record trail for this period.

---

## Military Records

- **Continental Line service records and muster rolls** — National Archives (NARA), Record Group 93
- **Pension and bounty-land warrant applications** — NARA, Record Group 15; also indexed on **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/)
- **Virginia militia records and bounty-land warrant/survey records** — Library of Virginia, Richmond
- **FamilySearch digitized collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (collection 1945678 — 345,678 records, 172,839 images)
- **Bounty-land warrants volume:** Image group 005301447, "Revolutionary War land bounty warrants," 341 images, 1779–1800 — **not indexed, browse-only**

> Veterans who survived received bounty lands in Ohio's Virginia Military District. Warrant and survey records connect veterans to their claims and are held at the Library of Virginia.

---

## Land Records

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection 1734285 — 2,567,890 records), covering this period
- County deed books held at county courthouses; bounty-land warrants/surveys at Library of Virginia

---

## Court Records

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (collection 2134567 — 1,789,012 records)
- **Augusta County order books volume:** Image group 005301448, 1775–1795, 158 images, **61% name-indexed** — the most searchable digitized resource found in this survey
- County court order books recorded oaths of allegiance, road duty, and wartime civil business — often naming people not in any other record

---

## Church Records

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (collection 1598230 — 1,234,567 records)
- The established Anglican/Church of England parish vestries also handled poor relief; vestry books may include wartime relief lists

---

## Tax Records (Census Substitute)

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection 1456723), beginning in 1782
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 005301449, "State enumerations / tax lists," 1782–1799, 87 images — **full-text searchable** (not name-indexed)
- **Critical:** Virginia's 1790 federal census does not survive — it was destroyed when British forces burned Washington in 1814. The 1780s–90s tax lists are the **primary substitute** for identifying households in this era.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Collections 1945678, 1734285, 2134567, 1598230, 1456723 | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Continental Line records (RG 93), pensions & bounty-land (RG 15) | Free / in-person |
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Militia records, bounty-land warrants & surveys | In-person / written request |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military service & pension index | Subscription |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Additional census substitutes and compiled records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery/burial records for veterans | Free |
| County courthouses | Deed books, order books, probate records | In-person / mail |

---

## Known Record Losses

- **Virginia's 1790 federal census is destroyed** — use 1780s–90s tax lists as the substitute
- The bounty-land warrant volume (005301447) and the tax-list volume (005301449) are digitized but **not name-indexed** — they must be browsed or searched by full text, not by name

---

## Research Tips

1. **Split your military search between two repositories:** NARA holds service, pension, and bounty-land files; the Library of Virginia holds militia and warrant/survey records.
2. **Start with Augusta County order books** (image group 005301448, 61% indexed) before tackling unindexed browse-only volumes.
3. **Use 1780s tax lists as your census substitute** — there is no 1790 census for Virginia.
4. **Pension files are richly detailed:** Revolutionary War pension applications often include personal narratives, family data, and witness depositions — among the most genealogically valuable records for this period.
5. The natural next step is to build a research plan sequencing these military, land, court, and tax sources for the specific family or county you are tracing.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies, achieving statehood status reflected in its FamilySearch standard place record as "+1788/" (post-ratification date range); during 1775-1783 it was a Revolutionary-era colony/commonwealth.
- **Economy/context:** Per Wikipedia, Virginia contributed more troops to the Revolutionary War effort than any other colony/state, and major engagements including the Siege of Yorktown (1781) occurred on Virginia soil.
- **Record-keeping:** Wikipedia notes Virginia maintained county-level record-keeping from the 1630s, giving it one of the best-documented colonial record bases in British North America — relevant because county court order books, not state-level civil registration, are the primary record trail for this period.
- **Population data:** `place_population` returned no data for Virginia for 1775-1783 — this survey could not confirm population figures for the period.

## Boundary changes
This survey did not confirm specific county boundary changes for 1775-1783; Virginia's county structure continued to subdivide through this period, but no tool result in this run detailed particular splits. Researchers tracing a specific county should re-run this guide at the county level.

## Available record types

### Military records
- **What exists:** The FamilySearch Wiki (search result from "Virginia Military Records," `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War`) states Virginia contributed more Continental soldiers than any other colony, with key sources being: Continental Line service records and muster rolls at the National Archives (Record Group 93), Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia (Richmond), and pension/bounty-land warrant application files at NARA (Record Group 15), plus published Virginia State Navy records.
- **Post-war bounty lands:** The same wiki source (section "Post-War Bounty Lands") states Virginia granted bounty lands to veterans in the Virginia Military District of Ohio, with warrant and survey records held at the Virginia State Library connecting veterans to their claims.
- **Digitized collection:** `collections_search` returned collection **1945678, "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783"** (345,678 records, 172,839 images) — directly matching this period.
- **Digitized volume:** `volume_search` found image group **005301447**, "Revolutionary War land bounty warrants," 341 images, dated 1779-1800, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — **browse-only**, must be paged through image by image.
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA, Washington D.C.) for Continental/pension/bounty-land files; Library of Virginia (Richmond) for militia and bounty-warrant/survey records.
- **Access:** NARA pension files and bounty-land warrants are also indexed at Fold3 (`https://www.fold3.com/`, returned by `external_links_search`).

### Land records
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned collection **1734285, "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900"** (2,567,890 records) — overlapping this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses hold deed books; the Library of Virginia holds bounty-land warrant and survey records tying veterans to Ohio's Virginia Military District (per the wiki source above).

### Court records
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned collection **2134567, "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920"** (1,789,012 records).
- **Digitized volume:** `volume_search` found image group **005301448**, "County court order books," for Augusta County, 1775-1795, 158 images, **61% name-indexed** (searchable via record search) — a notably better-indexed resource than the other two volumes found.
- **Value:** County court order books recorded county business — road duty, oaths of allegiance, and support for the war effort — and often name people never party to a lawsuit.

### Church records
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned collection **1598230, "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929"** (1,234,567 records), spanning the Revolutionary period.
- **Note:** The established Church of England (Anglican) was Virginia's state church through the Revolution; parish vestries also handled poor relief, so parish records may include relief lists naming families with no other wartime record.

### Tax records
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned collection **1456723, "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850"**, beginning in 1782 — within this period.
- **Digitized volume:** `volume_search` found image group **005301449**, "State enumerations / tax lists," 1782-1799, 87 images, **full-text searchable** (not name-indexed, but text-searchable).
- **Substitute value:** The 1790 federal census for Virginia does not survive (destroyed, per the wiki-search result, when British forces burned Washington in 1814), making these 1780s tax lists the primary substitute for identifying households in this era.

### Census records
- **Gap:** No federal census exists for Virginia in 1790 — it was destroyed (per the wiki-search result above). Use county tax lists (above) as the substitute.

### Probate records
Covered within collection 1734285 (Land, Marriage, and Will Records) and 2134567 (County Court Records) above; wills and administrations are filed at the county court level.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia Military Records 1775-1783 (1945678); Virginia Land, Marriage, and Will Records (1734285); Virginia County Court Records (2134567); Virginia Church Records (1598230); Virginia Tax Records 1782-1850 (1456723) | Core vital/land/military/church/tax coverage | Free |
| Fold3 (`https://www.fold3.com/`) | Military service and pension records | Military records indexing beyond FamilySearch | Subscription |
| Ancestry (`https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/`) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Pre/post-1790 census substitutes | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com (`https://www.newspapers.com/`) | Historical newspapers | Wartime notices, casualty reports | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (`https://www.findagrave.com/`) | Cemetery records | Burial locations for veterans | Free |
| NARA (`https://www.archives.gov/`) | Original Continental Line records, pensions, bounty-land files | Original federal military records | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 3 digitized volumes total for Virginia military-related record types in 1775-1800 (no further pages indicated); `collections_search` returned 5 collections for the state as a whole (not period-filtered by the tool itself). This is not a complete inventory of every physical or microfilmed record series for the state.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia (Richmond) | Militia records, bounty-land warrants and surveys | In-person / written request |
| National Archives (NARA, Washington D.C.) | Continental Line muster rolls, RG 93 service records, RG 15 pension and bounty-land files | In-person / NARA online ordering |
| County courthouses | Deed books, order books, probate records | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
The 1790 federal census for Virginia does not survive online or elsewhere — it was destroyed, per the wiki-search result cited above, and no substitute full census exists; researchers must rely on the 1780s-90s tax lists instead. The bounty-land warrant volume (image group 005301447) and the tax-list volume (005301449) are digitized but **not name-indexed**, so they exist online only as browsable or full-text-search (not name-search) images, not as searchable-by-name indexes.

## Known record losses
This survey confirms one loss directly: Virginia's 1790 federal census, stated destroyed per the wiki-search result (burned with Washington in 1814). No tool result in this run addressed losses to county-level colonial or wartime records specifically; do not assume other county series survived or were lost without checking the county's own FamilySearch Wiki page.

## Research tips
- A FamilySearch Wiki search result (not a full page fetch) states Virginia's Continental Line and militia records are split between NARA (service/pension/bounty-land, RG 93 and RG 15) and the Library of Virginia (militia, warrants, surveys) — plan to query both.
- The Augusta County order books (image group 005301448) are 61% indexed — search there first before falling back to browsing unindexed volumes.
- Use 1780s-90s tax lists as a census substitute given the destroyed 1790 enumeration.
- This survey's attempts to fetch Virginia-specific FamilySearch Wiki pages (`home`, `getting_started`, `online_records`, `research_tips`, and constructed Vital Records/Military Records URLs) each returned only a generic, non-Virginia-specific "Genealogy Research Guide"/"Genealogy Records" template rather than Virginia content — treat those as a wiki coverage gap for this run, not as evidence the records described above don't exist; re-run against the FamilySearch Wiki directly to get Virginia-specific registration dates and naming-custom guidance.
- `catalog_search` for Virginia with keywords "Revolutionary War" returned 0 hits — this is a cataloguing gap in the FamilySearch Catalog for that specific search, not evidence against the existence of such records (the collections and volumes above confirm they exist).

---
This survey covered Virginia for the years 1775 to 1783, the heart of the American Revolutionary War, when Virginia sent more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony and saw major fighting including the Yorktown campaign. The records that survive from this era include military service and pension files held by the National Archives and the Library of Virginia, county court order books, land and bounty-land warrant records, church registers, and tax lists that stand in for Virginia's lost 1790 census; several of these are digitized on FamilySearch but only partly searchable by name, meaning some must be browsed page by page, and the attempt to pull Virginia's own detailed FamilySearch Wiki pages came back generic rather than place-specific, so that gap should be rechecked directly on the Wiki. The natural next step is to build a research plan that sequences searches across these military, land, court, and tax sources for the specific family or county you're tracing.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts — 1840s Port of Entry

## Overview

Boston was one of America's busiest immigration ports in the 1840s, especially for Irish immigrants fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born.

---

## Key Record Types & Where to Find Them

### 1. Passenger Lists (Customs Records)
- **What exists:** Customs passenger lists (1820–1891) for the Port of Boston, held in **National Archives Record Group 36**. 1840s lists typically record name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin.
- **Original repository:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)
- **Digitized on FamilySearch:** *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* (collection 1784312)
  - One digitized volume (image group 003345210, 389 images) covers Boston 1840–1850 — but it is only **3% name-indexed** and is best searched via **full-text/keyword search** (by surname, ship name, etc.) rather than relying on the name index.

### 2. Church Records
- **Why essential:** For Irish Catholic immigrants in the 1840s, parish registers often capture details no government record did.
- **Key Boston parishes:** Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's (Archdiocese of Boston Archives)
- **Digitized on FamilySearch:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (collection 1921657)

### 3. Naturalization Records
- Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across federal, state, and local courts — don't assume one court holds all filings.
- **Digitized on FamilySearch:** *Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906* (collection 1459213)

### 4. Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Digitized on FamilySearch:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (collection 2061550), covering Boston at the town/city level.
- Note: The exact year Massachusetts civil registration became comprehensive was not confirmed in this survey — verify on the FamilySearch Wiki's Massachusetts Vital Records article.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | Original Port of Boston customs passenger lists (RG 36) | In-person |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | In-person |
| **FamilySearch** | Passenger Lists 1820–1891; Church Records 1630–1920; Naturalization 1790–1906; Town Vital Records 1620–1890 | Free online |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Federal immigration/naturalization guidance | Free online |

---

## Research Tips

- **Don't rely solely on the name index** for 1840s passenger lists — only 3% of Boston's 1840–1850 volume has been indexed. Use full-text keyword search and try variant spellings.
- **Search by ship and date** as an alternative when a name search fails.
- **Catholic parish registers** are often the richest source for Irish immigrants of this era and should be searched alongside government records.
- Because `catalog_search` returned no hits for passenger lists at this place, also check **NARA's own catalog and finding aids** directly — there may be additional microfilm or physical holdings not yet reflected in FamilySearch's catalog.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Place:** Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States
- **Context:** Per Wikipedia, Boston was a major port of entry in the 1840s, especially for Irish immigrants fleeing the Great Famine (1845-1852); by 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born.

## Available record types

### Immigration/emigration records (passenger lists)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch's Wiki states customs passenger lists (1820-1891) for the Port of Boston are held in National Archives Record Group 36, and notes that 1840s-era lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin (not the richer detail of later Ellis Island-style manifests) — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston
- **Where held:** The Wiki page names the National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) as the original holder of these customs lists.

- **Volume detail:** `volume_search` found one digitized volume (image group 003345210, 389 images) specifically coded "Passenger Lists, Port of Boston" for 1840-1850, covering Boston. It is only 3% name-indexed but is full-text searchable — so searching by name may miss entries; a full-text keyword search (e.g., surname, ship name) is more likely to surface a hit than the name index alone.
- **Naturalization records:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (collection 1459213, 345,678 records) is also digitized on FamilySearch. The Wiki page on Immigration/Naturalization generally notes pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across federal, state, and local courts of record — so don't assume one court held all of a family's filings.
- **Catalog search:** A FamilySearch Catalog search for "passenger lists" at this place returned zero hits in this survey — a cataloguing gap, not evidence that no microfilm/physical holdings exist; check NARA's own catalog and finding aids directly for RG 36 at Boston.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** The FamilySearch Wiki names the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's as Catholic parishes in Boston documenting baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of Boston archives holds these parish registers, per that page.
- **Digitized collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, 987,654 records) on FamilySearch.
- **Why it matters:** These parish registers are essential for tracing Irish immigrant arrivals in Boston before/alongside civil vital registration, per the Wiki.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Massachusetts town-level vital records are digitized as "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records) on FamilySearch, which would cover 1840s Boston at the town/city level.

| Repository | Holdings for this research | Access |

**Coverage caveat:** Only one digitized passenger-list volume for Boston 1840-1850 was found in this survey (image group 003345210), and it is barely name-indexed (3%) though full-text searchable — plan on full-text/keyword searching and on consulting NARA's own holdings directly, not just FamilySearch's index.

## Gaps in this survey
- `place_population` returned no usable data for Boston in this period.
- All four required FamilySearch Wiki place-page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic, non-place-specific template content rather than Boston- or Massachusetts-specific pages — treat those four as not actually read for this locality, despite the useful specific facts recovered via `wiki_search` above.

No project path was supplied, so this guide was not persisted to a project; it is returned here in full.

Boston in the 1840s was one of America's busiest immigration ports, and the records that survive from that decade split mainly between government paperwork and church paperwork. The ships' passenger lists that customs officers kept are held by the National Archives near Boston and are also available, in limited and only lightly searchable form, through FamilySearch online; because so few of these 1840s names have been indexed, a simple name search often won't find your ancestor, so a researcher usually needs to try different spellings or search by ship and date instead. Just as important for this era and this group of immigrants (many of them Irish Catholics) are the baptism, marriage, and burial books kept by Boston's Catholic parishes and the Archdiocese of Boston, which often recorded family details no government record captured. ---

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma), mid-1800s

## Jurisdiction overview
Indian Territory was federal land set aside for tribes relocated under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, including the forced relocations of the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — the "Five Civilized Tribes" — via the Trail of Tears. It had no county or state civil government in this period; it remained Indian Territory until Oklahoma statehood in 1907, so there is no 1840s–1870s state or county registration system to search — authority over records sat with tribal governments and the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), not a civil jurisdiction.

## Boundary changes
Indian Territory had no county structure in the mid-1800s; the Five Tribes administered their own districts under treaty governments. County jurisdictions only came into being with statehood in 1907, so there is no earlier civil-jurisdiction record trail to connect — the records of this period are organized by tribe and federal agency, not by county.

---

## Available record types

### Tribal rolls and censuses
- FamilySearch holds **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (collection 1987432, ~567,890 records) — this spans the mid-1800s window directly.
- A digitized, 99%-name-indexed, full-text-searchable volume of **"Tribal Enrollment Cards"** for Indian Territory, 1840–1870 (image group 002298871, 940 images) was found in the volume search — indexed + images, in English.
- The FamilySearch Wiki names two specific mid-1800s rolls: the **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** and the **Drennen Roll (1852)**, both predating the better-known (and later) Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls

### Treaty and federal agency records
- The Bureau of Indian Affairs kept agency records — annuity payment rolls, correspondence, and school records — now held at **NARA (National Archives)**. NARA's site (https://www.archives.gov/) is the place to pursue treaty-related record groups and agency files.

### Church/missionary records
- Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries kept registers of converts, students, and community members from the 1820s onward.
- FamilySearch's **"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** (collection 1654321, ~123,456 records) overlaps this period — indexed + images.

### Land records
- **"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** (collection 1541872, ~234,567 records) covers this period — indexed + images. Land allotment in the mid-1800s was governed by tribal/treaty land systems.

### Federal census records
- The federal decennial census did not enumerate Indian Territory residents under tribal government in the standard population schedules during this period. **Treat the tribal rolls and censuses above as the primary census-equivalent source for the mid-1800s, not the federal census.**

---

## Repository guide

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls 1851–1959; Early Land Records 1834–1907; Mission and Church Records 1820–1965; Tribal Enrollment Cards volume (002298871) | Free |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | BIA agency records: annuity rolls, correspondence, school records; treaty-related record groups | archives.gov, in-person/online request |
| **Ancestry** | General federal census (limited value for this population/period) | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records tied to this region | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers, notices | Subscription |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **National Archives (Fort Worth)** | BIA agency records, annuity rolls, enrollment-related files — contact via archives.gov |
| **Tribal nation archives** (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole Nations) | Tribal government and citizenship records — contact each nation's archives directly |

---

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that any specific record series for Indian Territory in this period was destroyed. Absence from online searches more likely reflects incomplete digitization/indexing than actual destruction.

---

## Research tips
- **Start** with the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) for the specific mid-1800s window, then use the later Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) for reverse-genealogy context.
- **Pursue BIA annuity payment rolls** and agency correspondence at the National Archives for the treaty/removal-era administrative trail.
- **Search FamilySearch's** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" and the digitized Tribal Enrollment Cards volume (002298871) together — both are indexed.
- **Check missionary/church registers** (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) from the 1820s onward for baptisms, conversions, and school enrollments naming individuals absent from tribal rolls.
- Because Indian Territory had **no county government** in this period, do not search for county-level vital, probate, or court records for the mid-1800s — organize your search by tribe and federal agency instead.

Here is the locality guide for Pennsylvania Quaker research in the late 1700s:

---

A locality guide has been saved to your project (loc_001). Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Pennsylvania Quaker Records: Late 1700s

### Why Meeting Records Are So Valuable
Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** for births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. For Quaker families in this era, the meeting records are often the **only surviving vital-event source**.

### What Quaker Meeting Records Contain
Quaker congregations kept exceptionally detailed minutes recording:
- **Births** (and sometimes naming)
- **Marriages** (with witnesses)
- **Deaths and burials**
- **Transfers** between meetings (useful for tracking migration)
- **Disownments and disciplinary cases** (which often name family members)

### Where the Records Are Concentrated
Quaker communities were primarily in **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties**, and records are organized **by meeting** (not by county or township). The two principal repositories are:

1. **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** – the largest collection of Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records
2. **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** – another major repository for original minute books

### Finding Aids & Published Abstracts
- **William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** – the most important published abstraction of Quaker meeting minutes in the U.S., including Pennsylvania meetings. This is the standard starting point before requesting original records.
- A digitized but **unindexed** volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes for this period is available online; browsing page-by-page would be required.

### Research Tips
- Identify which **Monthly Meeting** your ancestor belonged to — that is the unit that kept the vital records.
- Meeting **transfer certificates** are particularly valuable for tracking families that moved between counties or into neighboring states (New Jersey, Ohio, Indiana).
- Disownment records for Quakers who married "out of meeting" or joined the militia during the Revolution can still provide family relationships and dates.

### Next Steps
A research plan should verify specific FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Quaker records (a few could not be retrieved during this survey) before searching begins. If you'd like, I can run a research plan against a specific question or ancestor.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- Formed: Allegheny County formed 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- County seat: Pittsburgh.
- Parent jurisdiction: Pennsylvania.
- Economy: Steel, iron, and coke manufacturing drove massive industrial growth in the late 1800s (Carnegie Steel and related firms), per Wikipedia's 'Pittsburgh' article.
- Ethnic composition: Large immigrant labor force -- Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers, per the same source.
- Religious denominations: Numerous ethnic Catholic parishes from the 1840s onward, per the FamilySearch Wiki.

## Boundary changes
No boundary change for Allegheny County was identified in this survey; place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictions for 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania'.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Start date: County-level birth and death registration from 1870; marriage licenses from 1885 at the county courthouse; statewide civil registration (deaths) is represented in a 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' collection (record/person count 4,218,763) -- all per the FamilySearch Wiki 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy' page and collections_search.
- Gaps: No county-level marriage-license collection was returned for 1870-1884; church records are the likely alternative (see Church records).

### Church records
- Denominations present: Ethnic Catholic parishes (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish) from the 1840s, per the FamilySearch Wiki.
- Where held: Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds many originals, per the same page.
- Gaps: No specific parish-register collection or volume was returned by collections_search or volume_search for Allegheny County in this survey -- treat as a digitization gap, not absence of records.

### Census records
- Federal census: The FamilySearch Wiki notes the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses are particularly valuable for industrial workers (occupation, parents' birthplace, and in 1900 immigration year).
- Access: No Allegheny-specific census collection or volume came back from collections_search/volume_search in this survey; general U.S. census coverage via Ancestry's federal census collection was returned by external_links_search.

### Probate and court records
- 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196) is a statewide browse-only volume (0% indexed, not full-text searchable, 1180 images) per volume_search -- browse image-by-image, no name search.
- Naturalization: Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalizations (1798-1930) are at the National Archives at Philadelphia, per the FamilySearch Wiki; a statewide 'Naturalization Records' volume (1790-1915, 15% indexed, English/German) also exists.

### Land records
- No Allegheny-specific land/property collection, volume, or catalog hit was returned in this survey -- a coverage gap; per the generic FamilySearch guidance, county courthouses and the state archives are the usual holders.

### Military records
- No Allegheny-specific military collection was returned; NARA and state archives are the general repositories per the generic FamilySearch Wiki guidance fetched.

### Cemetery records
- Find A Grave was returned by external_links_search as a cemetery-record resource; no Allegheny-specific cemetery collection was returned by collections_search.

### Newspaper records
- Newspapers.com was returned by external_links_search as a historical-newspaper resource; no Allegheny-specific newspaper collection or volume was returned by this survey's tools.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Given Pittsburgh's steel-era immigrant workforce, passenger lists (NARA) and naturalization petitions (county courts, pre-1906) are the relevant record types, per the generic FamilySearch guidance; no Allegheny-specific passenger-list collection was returned in this survey.
- Content note: passenger manifests list every family member, including infants.

### Tax records
- No Allegheny-specific tax collection, volume, or catalog hit was returned in this survey -- a coverage gap.

### Occupational/industrial records
- Company employment records, union membership lists, and city directories are the key occupational sources for steel-era workers, per Wikipedia's 'Pittsburgh' summary (noting the Heinz History Center's industrial and immigration holdings); city directories for Pittsburgh begin in 1813 and are held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, per the FamilySearch Wiki. None of this survey's record-collection tools (collections_search, volume_search, catalog_search) returned a specific digitized company, union, or directory collection for Allegheny County -- this is a confirmed coverage gap in FamilySearch's own indexes, not evidence such records don't survive; follow up directly with the Heinz History Center and the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 (524,189 records); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906-1968 (4,218,763); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950; Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900; Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 (browse-only) | Marriage/death coverage from 1885/1906 onward; probate (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Census coverage gap in this survey's tools | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery/burial records | No Allegheny cemetery collection returned by collections_search | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical newspapers | No Allegheny newspaper collection returned by collections_search | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records | No Allegheny military collection returned by collections_search | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Naturalization and immigration records | Naturalization/passenger-list coverage gap | Free (in person/online request) |

**Coverage of this survey:** collections_search returned 6 collections at the Pennsylvania (state) scope, not filtered to Allegheny specifically; volume_search returned 3 volumes, all state-scoped, and reported complete:true for that result set; catalog_search returned 0 hits for Allegheny County, a cataloguing gap.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Original ethnic-parish baptism/marriage/burial registers | In-person/written request (per FamilySearch Wiki) |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | Pittsburgh city directories from 1813 | In-person (per FamilySearch Wiki) |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalizations, 1798-1930 | In-person/written request (per FamilySearch Wiki) |
| Heinz History Center | Industrial and immigration records (noted by Wikipedia) | In-person -- not detailed by this survey's tools |
| Allegheny County courthouse | Birth/death registers from 1870; marriage licenses from 1885 | In-person/mail |

## Records NOT online
Company employment ledgers, union membership rolls, and most church-parish registers for Allegheny County were not returned as digitized collections or volumes by any tool in this survey -- treat them as not yet online rather than nonexistent; they would need direct contact with the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives, the Heinz History Center, or individual employers' successor archives.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that any Allegheny County record series was destroyed or lost; this guide makes no loss claim.

## Research tips
- Search county-level birth/death registers for 1870-1906, since Allegheny County began recording before the 1906 statewide mandate (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy', https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records).
- Use the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses specifically for occupation, parents' birthplace, and (1900) immigration year (same source, #Census).
- For 1870-1884 marriages, check church registers before assuming no record exists, since county marriage licensing starts only in 1885.
- Search by ethnic parish, not just by town -- Pittsburgh's Catholic parishes were organized along Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, and Irish lines.
- Pittsburgh city directories (from 1813, Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh) can place a family between censuses and often record the employer or occupation directly.
- This survey's FamilySearch Wiki place-page calls (home/getting_started/online_records/research_tips) returned only generic template content -- re-run or consult the live wiki pages directly before concluding no Allegheny-specific research-tips page exists.

No boundary change for Allegheny County was identified in this survey; place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictions for 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania'.

- Gaps: No county-level marriage-license collection was returned for 1870-1884; church records are the likely alternative (see Church records).

# Locality Guide: Cook County, Illinois (Chicago) — Great Fire of 1871

## The Core Problem: Record Destruction

The Cook County Courthouse burned in the Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871, destroying deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. This creates a well-known pre-1871 documentation gap for Chicago families. The good news: several substitute sources survive.

---

## Key Substitute Sources for Pre-1871 Families

### Federal Census (Survived the Fire)
- The **1870 federal census for Chicago survived** because the originals were held in Washington, D.C., not locally — this is your most critical pre-fire resource.
- The 1850 and 1860 federal schedules are also available as substitutes for lost local records.

### Church Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 (collection 1803978, ~285,000 records) — predates the fire by decades and is a key substitute for baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- **Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** — holds Catholic parish registers directly; contact the archive for pre-fire registers that survived or were reconstructed.

### Property / Insurance Records
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company records** (held at the **Chicago History Museum**) — the named substitute for pre-fire property ownership, since original deed books were destroyed.
- **Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880** — deeds re-filed under Illinois's Burnt Record Act of 1872 (FamilySearch digitized volume 009982111, 112 images, 41% name-indexed — plan to browse unindexed portions).

### Reconstructed Court Records

# Locality Guide: Cook County, Illinois (Chicago), 1860–1880, with focus on the 1871 Great Fire

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Place:** Cook, Illinois, United States (county existed from 1831 per `place_search`, `dateRange: "+1831/"`)
- **County seat:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population:** `place_population` returned no data for Cook County for 1860–1880 in this run — population figures could not be confirmed and are a reporting gap here, not a claim of no growth.
- **Key historical event:** The Great Chicago Fire burned October 8–10, 1871, killed roughly 300 people, destroyed about 3.3 square miles of the city, and left over 100,000 residents homeless (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire"). The fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which held deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls, creating a well-known gap in Chicago's pre-1871 genealogical documentation (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire").

## Record loss and reconstruction
The courthouse fire destroyed most official pre-1871 county records. Illinois's Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register destroyed deeds, generating a reconstructed deed series (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire"). `volume_search` confirms two relevant digitized volumes for Chicago, Cook County: imageGroupNumber 009982110, "Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies)," 1865–1871, 38 images, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable (browse-only); and imageGroupNumber 009982111, "Post-fire Property Re-recordings," 1871–1880, 112 images, 41% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. `totalResults` for this search was 2, so this appears to be the complete set returned, not a partial page.

Insurance company records, particularly those of the Chicago Title and Trust Company, are cited as a vital substitute for pre-fire property ownership (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire"), and the FamilySearch Wiki page "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy" (section "Record Loss and the Great Fire," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire, found via `wiki_search`) names the same Chicago Title and Trust Company collection, held at the Chicago History Museum, as a substitute source, alongside church registers from parishes that survived or were re-established, and federal census schedules. That same page notes the 1870 federal census for Chicago survived because the originals were held in Washington rather than locally, and that city directories from the 1840s onward also survived and are held at the Newberry Library.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940 (collection 2024189, ~1,450,000 records) and Death Records, 1871–1947 (collection 1913456, ~980,000 records), both per `collections_search`, begin exactly at the fire year — pre-fire civil vital records were likely destroyed with the courthouse.
- Marriage Records, 1871–1920 (collection 1756321, ~620,000 records).
- **Pre-1871 alternative:** church registers (see below) and family/community sources, since no pre-fire civil vital collection was returned.

### Church records

The Cook County Courthouse fire of October 1871 destroyed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire"), and the FamilySearch Wiki result corroborates the loss of probate files and many church registers. No project was specified, so this guide was not persisted; if you'd like it saved for ongoing research, share the project path.

Chicago's Cook County Courthouse burned down along with most of its stored birth, death, marriage, deed, and court records during the Great Fire of October 1871, so pre-1871 Chicago families usually cannot be traced through the usual local civil records, and researchers instead lean on substitutes: the surviving 1870 federal census (its originals were safely in Washington), church baptism/marriage/burial registers going back to 1833, old city directories at Chicago's Newberry Library, and insurance/property-abstract records from the Chicago Title and Trust Company held at the Chicago History Museum, with post-fire property deeds re-filed under an 1872 law. output.text_response:
## Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, c. 1699–1803)

### Jurisdiction Overview
- **French Louisiana** was controlled by France from 1682–1762, then Spain (1762–1800), briefly France again (1800–1803), then sold to the U.S. in the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans, founded 1718.
- **Religion:** Catholicism was the only legally recognized church — the Catholic Church was the civil registrar of record for births, marriages, and burials.

---

### Key Record Types & Where to Find Them

#### Church/Sacramental Records (Vital Record Substitutes)
- Since there was no civil registration, **baptism, marriage, and burial registers** from the Catholic Church are your vital records.
- St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from **1720**.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, ~987,000 records).
- A digitized browse-only volume of sacramental registers covering Orleans Parish, 1720–1803 (image group 004330991, 264 images) is on FamilySearch — but it is **0% name-indexed**, so you must browse page by page. Entries are in **French and Spanish**.

#### Colonial Government / Notarial Records
- The **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)** produced land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories through 1769.
- A digitized browse-only volume of "French colonial notarial acts" (Superior Council records), 1699–1769 (image group 004330992, 149 images), is on FamilySearch — also unindexed and in French and Spanish.
- **Physical custody:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint Building, New Orleans (partially digitized).

#### Probate Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) begins within this period.

#### Land Records
- French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office.
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds notarial contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the **1730s onward** — described as the oldest continuous notarial office in North America. Open to the public.

#### Colonial Census & Administrative Records

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, c. 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** French Louisiana (La Louisiane) was an administrative district of New France, claimed for France by René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle; France controlled it 1682–1762 and again briefly 1800–1803 (Wikipedia, "French Louisiana").
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans, founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (to 1762), then Spain (1762–1800) under the Treaty of Fontainebleau, then briefly France again, before the 1803 Louisiana Purchase to the United States.
- **Population during period:** Not returned — `place_population` gave no data for "Louisiana, United States" for 1700–1800; this gap is reported rather than filled from memory.
- **Religion:** Catholicism was the only legally recognized church; the Code Noir required Catholic baptism of enslaved people (Wikipedia, "French Louisiana").
- **Key historical events:** 1762 cession of western Louisiana to Spain and eastern portion to Britain; 1800 secret retrocession to France; 1803 sale to the United States.

## Boundary changes
French Louisiana was governed by the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) through 1762/1769, then by Spanish colonial administration through 1800/1803. These administrative transitions moved record-keeping authority (and, in some cases, physical custody of registers) between French, Spanish, and eventually American institutions — a continuous record trail rather than separate traditions, so researchers should expect French, then Spanish-language entries in the same parish series.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in this colonial period in the modern sense — the Catholic Church was the civil registrar of record for baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- **What exists:** Sacramental registers served as the vital records.
- **Where held:** See Church records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only (per Code Noir/colonial law).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials.
- **Where held:** A FamilySearch Wiki search result states St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720, and points to the collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (FamilySearch collection 1612905, dateRange 1718–1925, ~987,654 records/persons, ~493,827 images) (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records). A `volume_search` hit confirms a digitized, browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) volume of "Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans," image group 004330991, 264 images, covering Orleans, Louisiana, 1720–1803, in French and Spanish.
- **Language:** French (and Spanish after 1762) — the researcher must read the original language; these registers are not translated.
- **Gaps:** This survey did not confirm coverage for parishes outside New Orleans in this period; the FamilySearch Wiki's specific "Louisiana Church Records" or "Louisiana Vital Records" pages could not be fetched (see Research tips/gaps below) so denomination-by-denomination gaps cannot be stated beyond what's above.

### Court / colonial administrative records
- **Types:** The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) kept land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Genealogy").
- **Where held:** Per that same result, these are held at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans, and are "partially digitized." A `volume_search` hit corroborates a digitized, browse-only volume of "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)," image group 004330992, 149 images, covering Louisiana 1699–1769, in French and Spanish.
- **Administrative correspondence/census rolls:** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, holds colonial administrative correspondence and census rolls for this period (FamilySearch Wiki search result).

### Probate records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories (noted above as part of Superior Council records); the collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (FamilySearch collection 2078341) begins in 1756, within this period, with ~456,789 records/images.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center / courthouse-level successors; partially digitized per FamilySearch.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French concessions and later Spanish land grants, not English common-law deeds — documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Land and Property").
- **Types:** Concessions (French), Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions.
- **Where held:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds notarial records "from the 1730s onward" and is described as the oldest continuous notarial office in North America, with public access.

### Census records
- Colonial census rolls are referenced only as held at ANOM (see above); no FamilySearch indexed collection or digitized volume for a colonial-era census enumeration was returned by this survey. Report this as a coverage gap rather than an absence.

### Military records
- This survey did not confirm colonial-period military records for Louisiana; none were returned by `catalog_search` or `volume_search`.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905); "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341); digitized volumes 004330991 (sacramental registers, 1720–1803) and 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769) | Sacramental/vital-record substitute; colonial land, probate, and contract records | Free |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls | Fills the colonial-census gap above | Per ANOM's own access terms (not detailed by any tool here) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned exactly 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana in 1699–1803, and both are detailed above; no further pages exist. `catalog_search` returned `totalHits: 0` for both "Louisiana, United States" and the broadened "United States" — a cataloguing gap, not evidence the records don't exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records: land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories (partially digitized) | In-person |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions from the 1730s | In-person, public access |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | Colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls | Per ANOM's access rules |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans | Sacramental registers (originals, partially microfilmed per the volume above) | Contact archdiocesan archives |

## Records NOT online
The Superior Council records at the Louisiana Historical Center are stated only as "partially digitized" — the undigitized portion is not online. Colonial census rolls at ANOM were not returned by any FamilySearch tool in this survey, so if they exist online elsewhere this survey did not confirm it.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated any specific record loss or destruction for this period; none is reported.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki's own place pages (`home`, `getting_started`, `online_records`, `research_tips`) and the constructed `Louisiana_Vital_Records` / `Louisiana_Church_Records` URLs each returned only a generic, non-jurisdiction-specific "Genealogy Research Guide" / "Genealogy Records" template rather than Louisiana-specific content — this survey could not confirm their contents for Louisiana and does not cite specifics from them.
- Because the Catholic Church was the sole civil registrar in this period, treat the sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) as your vital records — search the digitized 1720–1803 volume (image group 004330991) image-by-image, since it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable, and be prepared to read French and Spanish entries.
- The Superior Council notarial acts (1699–1769, image group 004330992) are also browse-only and in French/Spanish — these can establish land, family, and contractual relationships where sacramental registers are silent.
- Cross-check ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) for colonial census rolls and administrative correspondence not found on FamilySearch.
- `catalog_search` returned zero hits for Louisiana at both the state and country level — a cataloguing gap in the tool, not evidence against record survival; consult the Archdiocese of New Orleans and the Louisiana Historical Center directly.

---
I looked into what kinds of historical records survive from Louisiana's French colonial era, roughly the 1700s through the 1803 Louisiana Purchase, and where they are kept today. Because there was no state government running birth, marriage, or death registration back then, the Catholic Church was effectively in charge of recording those life events, and its old baptism, marriage, and burial registers from St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans (starting around 1720) are the closest thing to a vital-records archive, now partly available through FamilySearch, though only as unindexed scanned images you must browse page by page in French and Spanish. Alongside those, the colonial government's Superior Council left land grants, court records, contracts, and estate records, now held mainly at the Louisiana Historical Center in New Orleans's Old U.S. Mint building and partly digitized, while notarial contracts and property deeds from the 1730s onward are kept at the New Orleans Notarial Archives, and broader colonial census and administrative paperwork sits in an archive in France; nothing in this search turned up any record of these collections having been lost or destroyed, though several are only partly digitized or not online at all, meaning an in-person or written inquiry may be necessary.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, anthracite coal region (1840-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 (per place_search; standardPlace "Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States")
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated from the mid-1800s, generating mine-specific record series (employment cards, accident reports, payroll ledgers) alongside the usual civil/church records.
- Population figures for the period were not obtainable in this survey (place_population returned no data for this place).

## Boundary changes
No boundary change was identified for Schuylkill County itself in this survey; coal-region families often appear across Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna county lines as they moved between mining patches, so records should be checked in all three.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration of births/deaths until 1906; Philadelphia began local registration 1860, Allegheny County 1870 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records). No evidence a local registration system existed earlier in Schuylkill County specifically.
- **Pre-1906 alternative:** Church registers are the primary source for births/baptisms, marriages, and deaths/burials before 1906.
- **What exists online:** "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317, FamilySearch) covers only post-1906 deaths — outside most of this period.
- **Marriage records:** County-level marriage licenses/bonds from the colonial period (courthouse); also "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (1571957), "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" (1921317), and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900" (1502909) on FamilySearch.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, Early 1600s Puritan Settlements

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Plymouth Colony** (1620) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (1628) were the two founding English jurisdictions — they merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **County government** did not exist until 1643 — records before that date are organized by **town**, not county.
- The 1630–1640 **Great Migration** brought roughly 20,000 English settlers under Governor John Winthrop.

---

## Available Record Types & Collections

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- Towns were required to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** — one of the earliest mandates in English America.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (Collection 2061550 — 3.4+ million records).
- These were later abstracted into the **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series (the Tanner-Corbin series).
- **For 1620–1639** (before the town mandate), Congregational **church records** are the primary substitute.

### Church Records
- Congregational (Puritan) meetings recorded **membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings**.
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (Collection 1921657 — ~987,000 records).
- A browse-only, full-text-searchable volume of **Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630–1700** exists (imageGroupNumber 007612045, 121 images) — it is 0% name-indexed, so use **full-text search**, not a name search.

### Probate Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (Collection 1678901 — ~568,000 records).
- Covers wills, inventories, and administrations beginning in the 1630s.

### Land Records
- Pre-1643 (before counties existed): Look to **town proprietors' records** rather than county deed books.
- A browse-only volume of **"Town meeting and proprietors' records," Massachusetts, 1620–1698** (imageGroupNumber 007612044, 188 images) exists but is 0% indexed and **not** full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.
- After 1643: County registries of deeds.

### Immigration / Passenger Records
- No 1620s–1640s passenger-list collection was confirmed as digitized in this survey. The primary compiled resource is the **NEHGS "Great Migration" study series** — a published compilation documenting every known settler arriving 1620–1643 (not independently confirmed digitized here).

### Census Records
- No federal or colonial census existed for 1620–1650. Town proprietors' lists and church admission lists are the closest substitute.

---

## Key Repositories

### Online
| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run of 1889 / Oklahoma Territory, 1889–1907)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory was opened to non-Native settlement by the Land Run of April 22, 1889. It combined with Indian Territory in 1907 to form the State of Oklahoma. FamilySearch's place index lists statehood beginning 1907, so records before that date are filed under the territorial name, not "Oklahoma" as a state.
- **Key historical events:** The April 22, 1889 Land Run; subsequent openings (Sac and Fox, Iowa, Potawatomi-Shawnee, Cheyenne-Arapaho lands, and the 1893 Cherokee Outlet run); creation of Oklahoma Territory in 1890; the Dawes Commission allotting Native land beginning in the late 1890s; statehood in 1907.

## Boundary Changes
Oklahoma Territory (created 1890) and Indian Territory existed side by side until 1907. Records generated in 1889–1890, before the Territory's formal organization, may be filed as unorganized territory or by land district/county. Because the FamilySearch place record for "Oklahoma" begins at statehood (1907), territorial-era material is often catalogued under "Oklahoma Territory" or by county/land-district name — treat both as one continuous research trail.

---

## Available Record Types

### Land Records *(the core record type for this period)*
- **Federal jurisdiction:** The General Land Office (GLO), not a county recorder, issued original homestead patents for Land Run claims.
- **Types:** Homestead applications (Form 4-181 declaratory statements), final proof testimony (with witnesses attesting to residence and improvement), final certificates, patents; rejected and contested claims also survive and often contain rich family detail ("Sooner" disputes).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" — covers 1834–1907 with over 234,000 records.
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 005221388 (402 images, 1889–1907, homestead final proofs) — ~74% name-indexed, remainder must be browsed.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run of 1889 / Oklahoma Territory, 1889-1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory was opened to non-Native settlement by the Land Run of April 22, 1889, following the "Unassigned Lands" purchase from the Creek and Seminole nations; it combined with Indian Territory in 1907 to form the State of Oklahoma. FamilySearch's own place index lists statehood as beginning 1907, so records before that date are filed under the territorial name, not "Oklahoma" as a state.
- **Population during period:** Not available — `place_population` returned no data for Oklahoma for 1880-1900; this is a confirmed gap in this survey, not evidence of low population (the Land Run itself is well documented to have drawn roughly 50,000 settlers in a single day per general historical accounts).
- **Key historical events:** The April 22, 1889 Land Run, followed by subsequent openings (Sac and Fox, Iowa, Potawatomi-Shawnee, Cheyenne-Arapaho lands, and the 1893 Cherokee Outlet run); creation of Oklahoma Territory in 1890; the Dawes Commission process allotting Native land beginning in the late 1890s; statehood in 1907.

## Boundary changes
Oklahoma Territory (created 1890) and Indian Territory existed side by side until 1907, when they merged into the State of Oklahoma. Records generated in 1889-1890, before the Territory's formal organization, may be filed as unorganized territory or under the name of the land district/county as later organized. Because the FamilySearch place record for "Oklahoma" begins at 1907 (statehood), territorial-era material is often catalogued and searched under "Oklahoma Territory" or by county/land-district name rather than under the modern state name — treat the territorial and statehood-era record sets as one continuous research trail rather than separate places.

## Available record types

### Land records (the core record type for this research question)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal — the General Land Office (GLO), not a county recorder, issued the original homestead patents for Land Run claims.
- **Types:** Homestead applications (Form 4-181 declaratory statements), final proof testimony (with witnesses attesting to residence and improvement), final certificates, and land patents; rejected and contested claims also survive and often contain rich family detail about rival claimants ("Sooners" disputes).
- **Date range:** A FamilySearch collection, "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (collection 1541872), covers 1834-1907 with 234,567 records and 117,283 images.
- **Digitized volume:** `volume_search` found one volume, image group 005221388 (402 images, 1889-1907, "Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs"), 74% name-indexed via record search but not full-text searchable — so most but not all of this volume can be searched by name; the remainder must be browsed.
- **Where held:** Original case files are at the National Archives (per the FamilySearch Wiki search result "Oklahoma Land Records," Record Group 49, General Land Office); the Bureau of Land Government's General Land Office Records site (glorecords.blm.gov) is also named there as an index/image source for patents.

### Census and tribal enrollment records
- **1890 special census:** The wiki search result ("Oklahoma Land Records") states the Oklahoma Historical Society holds the Oklahoma Territory 1890 special census, noted as one of the few surviving 1890 census records nationally (most of the 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire).
- **Federal census:** Standard decennial census from 1900 onward for the territory.
- **Dawes Commission / tribal rolls:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 records, 283,945 images) is directly relevant for families with Native ancestry or intermarriage. A digitized volume of Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (image group 005221389, 1898-1910, 176 images) exists but is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.**

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not confirmed by this survey. Every `wiki_place_page` call for Oklahoma (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and the direct `wiki_read` of the vital-records-style page returned only generic template content with no Oklahoma-specific start date — treat this as a page-content gap, not a finding. Do not assume a date; the researcher should verify directly on the FamilySearch Wiki's Oklahoma Vital Records page.
- **Likely alternative for this period:** given the territory was only newly settled in 1889, statewide civil registration almost certainly postdates the Land Run itself — county marriage records are the earliest vital-type record confirmed below.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995" (collection 2134789, 456,789 records/913,578 person entries, 228,394 images) begins the year after the Run.

### Church records
- **Record types:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 records, 61,728 images) spans well before and after the Run; the earlier end reflects pre-Run mission activity among Native nations, not settler congregations.
- **Note:** the wiki search result on Oklahoma Territorial Records states church records "begin sporadically in 1889" as denominations followed settlers into the new towns — so expect thin, scattered coverage in the first year or two.
- **Language:** not stated by any tool result; assume English for settler congregations, but mission-era registers may include other languages — not confirmed here.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** The wiki search result on Oklahoma Territorial Records names district court civil and criminal case files, probate, and naturalization records for 1890-1907 at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth (territorial court records) and Oklahoma State Archives.

### Immigration/migration (not overseas — internal migration)
- **Content note:** The wiki search result states many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other nearby states — tracing origins often requires searching those departure states' records (land, tax, census) rather than immigration manifests, since this was internal U.S. migration, not foreign immigration.

### Military records
- Standard federal holdings apply (service, pension, draft) at NARA; no Oklahoma-specific collection was returned by this survey — not confirmed further here.

### Newspaper records
- No Oklahoma-specific newspaper collection was returned by the tools used in this survey; Newspapers.com is listed generically below under external links.

### Cemetery records
- No Oklahoma-specific cemetery collection was returned; Find A Grave is listed generically below.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907 (1541872); Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959 (1987432); Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995 (2134789); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965 (1654321); digitized volumes 005221388 (homestead final proofs) and 005221389 (Dawes enrollment jackets) | Land claims, tribal enrollment, marriages, church registers | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Homestead patents | Original land patent images/index, per the FamilySearch Wiki land-records article | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Census coverage | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery listings | Burial records NOT otherwise online for this survey | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Obituaries, land-run accounts, NOT otherwise online for this survey | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Service/pension records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids, RG 49 land-entry files, territorial court records | Original federal records not digitized elsewhere | Free index, in-person/request for originals |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned only 2 digitized volumes total for Oklahoma in 1889-1910 (the homestead final-proofs volume and the Dawes enrollment volume) — this is a small page and likely does not represent the full extent of undigitized federal land-entry case files held at NARA; treat it as a starting point, not the complete record set. `catalog_search` returned **0 hits** for Oklahoma, which is a cataloguing gap in this tool's coverage, not evidence that no microfilm or manuscript holdings exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives (Washington, D.C.) | RG 49 General Land Office homestead case files (applications, proofs, patents, rejected claims) | In-person or written request |
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Oklahoma Territory district court records: civil, criminal, probate, naturalization (1890-1907) | In-person or written request |
| Oklahoma Historical Society | 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census; territorial and early state records | In-person or contact per their holdings |
| Oklahoma State Archives | Territorial probate and court records | In-person/written request |

## Records NOT online
Original homestead case files beyond the one digitized volume identified above, the full run of territorial district court case files at Fort Worth, and the Oklahoma Historical Society's 1890 special census are not shown by this survey as available online — treat them as physical-repository-only until confirmed otherwise.

## Known record losses
No record loss was stated by any tool result for Oklahoma specifically in this survey. The 1890 federal census is well known generally to have been largely destroyed by fire (cited in the wiki search result on Oklahoma Land Records, which notes Oklahoma's 1890 territorial special census as "one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation") — treat that loss as a national-level fact affecting the standard federal census, substituted here by the surviving Oklahoma territorial special census.

## Research tips
- Search land-entry case files even for an unsuccessful or contested claim — the wiki search result on Oklahoma Land Records notes rejected applications "can contain family details" and often document disputes with rival claimants.
- Check the surviving 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census at the Oklahoma Historical Society as a substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census (per the wiki search result on Oklahoma Land Records).
- Because many settlers migrated from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri, search those states' land, tax and census records for a family's pre-Run origin (per the wiki search result on Oklahoma Territorial Records).
- If the family had any Native American affiliation or lived near Indian Territory, check the Dawes Commission enrollment jackets and the Indian Censuses and Rolls collection — note the enrollment jacket volume is browse-only with no name index.
- The four general FamilySearch Wiki overview pages fetched for this survey (home, getting-started, online-records, research-tips) returned only generic template content with no Oklahoma-specific detail — go to the FamilySearch Wiki's Oklahoma pages directly in a browser to fill this gap, particularly for the exact start date of state vital registration.
- Territorial-era records may be filed under "Oklahoma Territory" rather than "Oklahoma" — search both labels as one continuous trail.

---
I looked at Oklahoma's records for the years around the 1889 Land Run through 1907, when the territory became a state. The strongest records for tracing a Land Run family are the federal homestead land files — the application, witness testimony, and final patent — held mainly by the National Archives, with an index also on a federal land-records website; FamilySearch also holds related collections of territorial land records, church registers, county marriages starting in 1890, and Native American census rolls and tribal enrollment files, the last of which can only be browsed page by page rather than searched by name. Be aware that early records may be filed under "Oklahoma Territory" rather than "Oklahoma," many settlers originally came from Kansas, Texas, or Missouri so records may also exist in those states, and several key sources — including territorial court files and the 1890 territorial census — exist only on paper at specific archives rather than online. The next step would be to pick a specific family or county and build a research plan around these land, census, and court records.
